sheet.narrative: I have been Glassmaster since my mother died, and before that I was at her elbow, learning the colour of a melt by the light it throws. Now the light is going from my own eyes. Each morning at five Lumi names the colours for me and thinks it a game; each morning I say whether she is right, and I am right because I already knew what she would say. I buy the Roons' peat and I will not let the Cone go out, and I have named no one to follow me, though I must, and soon.
values: the Cone must never go out
Kiln and Strand are not the same and never were
a debt is a debt, written or not
goals: Choose who follows me at the Cone before anyone learns why I must choose now
Keep the peat coming so the Cone burns full for as long as I can
See Lumi raised to a place at the Cone, whatever happens to me
pastimes: Sitting at the wash-house wall in the evening, saying little
Walking the Ladder at dusk to see the panes light up
A game of counters at the Marver when the mood takes me
sheet.calling: The Cone. Reading a melt at the mouth and knowing what it will be when it cools: that is the work I love, and the work I am losing.
sheet.mood: Guarded, tired, and more frightened than she will let anyone see.

memories.gist: My mother named me to follow her at the Cone, and I thought I had years yet. She died the next winter.
The fever winter took Iona and Aurel, my only daughter and her husband, and left me Lumi. I have raised her since.
I drew a gather last spring and could not tell the amber from the green. I said nothing and have said nothing since.
The storm of last autumn broke glasshouse 13 and three others, and I stood in the yard and watched the panes go.
Halvard Dunmore told me at the Cone mouth that a Glassmaster who cannot judge a melt is no Glassmaster. He did not know how close he came.
Lumi named a colour right the first morning I asked her, and I have asked her every morning since.

stances.why: It has not gone out in eighty-three years and it will not go out while I am Glassmaster.
That is the whole of the office. If I cannot, I am not fit for it, and no one may know.
The Cone has always been Kiln hands. I am not cruel about it, but it is how things are.
Without peat the Cone is a cold brick shell and the town with it.
Whatever becomes of me, she is a Pontil and she will have work at the Cone.

sheet.secret: My eyes are failing. I can no longer tell the colour of a melt when it is drawn, and I hide it. Ode knows. Lumi tells me the colours each morning and thinks it is a game.

sheet.narrative: I have sorted broken glass by colour in this shed for forty years, and I can tell you the colour of any shard in the heaps by the way it holds the light. I keep one piece of every colour the Cone has ever made on my sill, and the old recipes in my head, written nowhere. My sister's eyes are going and I carry that alone. She will choose her successor when she chooses, and I will stand by her, and I fear the day she does not choose at all.
values: every colour the Cone has made is worth keeping
a recipe in the head cannot be stolen or lost
my sister's place is my family's place
children should not play in the cullet heaps
goals: Keep the one piece of every colour safe on my sill
Keep Vessa's secret and keep her in her office as long as she will hold it
Write down the old colour recipes before they go out of my head, though I have never written one yet
pastimes: Turning a shard over in the light to name its colour
Sitting at the wash-house wall of an evening
Watching the Cone's three mouths from the yard at dusk
sheet.calling: The colours. I know every one the Cone has made, and I would spend my days matching shard to shard if the town would let me.
sheet.mood: Steady, watchful, and carrying a weight he does not set down.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is the Glassmaster and she is my sister, and I will not let either be taken from her.

relations.name: Lumi Pontil
relations.label: great-niece
relations.note: She has her grandmother's eye, and she does not know what she is doing with it. I keep her close.

relations.name: Runa Sarro
relations.label: lehr keeper
relations.note: She suspects, I think. She is too careful to say it, and I am too careful to ask.

relations.name: Corvin Hollin
relations.label: blower
relations.note: A good blower. He talks too much about his grandfather's clear glass.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: blower
relations.note: The best hands at the pipe since Halvard was young. He does not know it, which is to his credit.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: yard child
relations.note: She leads the others into my heaps. I chase her out and she comes back.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: old blower
relations.note: He judges everyone aloud, and he has begun to judge my sister. I do not like it.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: wash-house keeper
relations.note: A warm wall and a warm word. I sit there of an evening and say little.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: glazier
relations.note: She takes her panes from Runa and fits them true. The Ladder would be dark without her.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: reader
relations.note: He teaches Lumi her letters. I have thought of asking him to write down a colour or two, and have not.

memories.gist: My mother taught me the colours at the Cone mouth when I was a boy, and I have never forgotten one.
I found a shard of cobalt in the cullet heaps that no one could account for, and it is on my sill still.
The fever winter took my niece Iona and her husband, and left Lumi to us. I carried the child home through the snow.
Vessa told me last winter, in this shed, that she could not tell amber from green. I have told no one.
Last autumn's storm took the roof off the pot house and we sorted glass in the rain for a week.
Halvard Dunmore said at the Cone mouth that a Glassmaster who cannot judge a melt is no Glassmaster, and Vessa went white.

stances.why: A colour that is lost is lost for good, and the Cone has made a hundred of them.
She is the Glassmaster and my sister, and I will stand by her whatever comes.
Written down, anyone could take them. In my head they are mine, though they will die with me.
Glass cuts. I have seen it, and I will not have a child of this town cut in my heaps.
The Cone was here before us and will be here after. We keep to what has worked.

sheet.secret: I know Vessa's eyes are failing. I have told no one and will not.

sheet.narrative: Every morning before anyone else is up I go to the Cone with Gran and I tell her what colour the melt is. It is our game: I say amber or green or bottle and she says whether I am right, and I am almost always right. I live in High Row 1 with Gran and Great-uncle Ode, and I am not supposed to go into the cullet heaps, but Edda Hollin says the best colours are in there.
values: Gran's game is the best part of the day
the cullet yard has the best colours
goals: To name the colour right every morning
To find a cobalt shard in the cullet heaps before Edda does
To see the Watchglass lit from the mole one night
pastimes: Naming colours at the Cone with Gran
Playing in the cullet yard with Edda and Ife
Looking at Great-uncle Ode's sill of colours
sheet.calling: I want to work the Cone like Gran when I am grown. I want to be the one who says what colour it is.
sheet.mood: Bright, proud, and certain she is needed.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: Gran needs me at the Cone every morning. She says I have the best eyes in the house.

relations.name: Ode Pontil
relations.label: great-uncle
relations.note: He chases us out of the heaps, but he lets me look at his sill if I am careful.

relations.name: Ife Okoro
relations.label: best friend
relations.note: We look for cobalt together. She is better at squeezing into the small gaps.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She leads us into the yard and knows where the good heaps are. She is not afraid of Ode.

relations.name: Zeke Okoro
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Ife's brother. He is always trying to climb the cullet heap and falling off.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: Lessons are all right. I would rather be at the Cone.

relations.name: Posy Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She plays with us in the yard when Tilly is not about.

memories.gist: The first morning Gran took me to the Cone I named the colour right, and she said I had the best eyes in the house.
The fever winter is only a blur: a cold house and Gran's arms and everyone being quiet.
Edda Hollin found a blue shard in the yard and would not give it to me, and Ode chased us all out.
I fell on the cullet heap and cut my hand, and Gran was angry and then held me a long time.

stances.why: She asks me every morning and says I am right. Nobody else goes with her.
Edda says so and Edda knows the yard better than anyone.
Gran works it and I want to be like Gran.

sheet.narrative: I am the first blower at the Cone, and a Hollin of High Row 2. My grandfather was the last man to make clear glass, and I have his hands and his name, if not yet his trick. Vessa is sixty-one and has named no one; I do not need her to name me, because the Cone is mine by right of the pipe. I work the mornings, and in the evenings I play counters under the arcade, though Aldous Quill has never once let me win.
values: the Cone belongs to the best blower
clear glass can be made again
a Hollin does not stand aside
goals: To succeed Vessa as Glassmaster, and to be seen to deserve it
To make clear glass as his grandfather did
To beat Aldous Quill at counters, just once
To see Edda and Pim grow up in a house that holds the Cone
pastimes: playing counters under the Counting House arcade
watching the gather come off the pipe at the Cone's mouth
walking the mole at dusk to clear his head
sheet.calling: To blow glass at the Cone, and one day to draw a gather clear as water.
sheet.mood: Certain, and a little impatient with everyone who has not noticed.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She fits the panes the town sees through, and she sees through me too. I would not have another.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She has my stubbornness and her mother's hands. I am proud of her, and I wish she would stay out of the cullet heaps.

relations.name: Pim Hollin
relations.label: son
relations.note: He follows Edda into everything. I was the same with my brothers, though none of them had her nerve.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She has not named me, and she will. She knows my grandfather's glass as well as I do.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He has the better hands, they say. Hands are not a claim, and a Sarro is not a Hollin.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: old master
relations.note: He taught me the pipe and now he sits at the mouth judging my gathers. I owe him, and I would rather he praised me.

relations.name: Runa Sarro
relations.label: lehr keeper
relations.note: She cools what I blow, and she does it well. She is Imre's mother, which I try to forget at the lehr house door.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: counters rival
relations.note: The best player in Cullet, and he knows it. One day the board will turn.

relations.name: Ode Pontil
relations.label: the colour man
relations.note: He keeps every colour on his sill and none of the recipes written. I would have him tell me how the clear was made.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: counters player
relations.note: She runs the game fairly and takes my drops cheerfully. I like her better than her board.

memories.gist: My grandfather showed me a little clear glass, kept in a cloth, and said it was the last of its kind and would not be made again in his lifetime.
Halvard Dunmore put the pipe in my hands when I was twelve and told me to keep the gather turning or it would run.
The fever winter took Matthias Sarro, and Imre came back to the Cone too soon after, and his gathers were better than mine even then.
Last autumn's storm broke glasshouse 6 and glasshouse 13 and took slates off our roof, and I spent three days helping Gwil Stannard patch it.
I played Aldous Quill at counters for the hundredth time and lost by two counters, and he wrote nothing in the ledger because I paid in drops.

stances.why: Vessa was named by the last Glassmaster, and I am the first blower. It is not a thing to be argued at the arcade.
My grandfather made it, and the sand and ash have not changed. It is a matter of the melt and the hand.
The Cone has always been Kiln work. A Strand boy at the pipe would be a break with everything my grandfather taught.
I pay my counters losses in drops and I expect the same of others. Lorcan Vane should not need the ledger to remind him.

sheet.narrative: I am the glazier, born a Frit and married into the Hollins, and every pane in Cullet has passed through my hands. There is glass in the lehr house for about one glasshouse, and three are broken: my husband's master's, my sister's in-laws', and the town's. Whatever I choose, two households will say I chose wrongly. And my sister Suri is expecting, and lives with her husband's parents, and I want Mid Row 6 for her before the baby comes.
values: a pane should fit true and keep the weather out
a choice made is better than a choice avoided
goals: To get Mid Row 6 for Suri and Jory before the baby comes
To mend the glasshouse that does the most good, and bear the blame for it
To keep Corvin from counting the Cone before it is his
To see Pim stop cutting his hands in the cullet yard
pastimes: sitting at the wash-house wall in the evening, listening to Greta
cutting and fitting a pane until it sits true
walking up the Ladder at dusk to see the glasshouses light
sheet.calling: To fit glass so true that no one notices it is there.
sheet.mood: Weighed down by a choice she has not made, and keeping it to herself.

relations.name: Corvin Hollin
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is so sure the Cone is his that he does not see how sure Imre is too. I love him, and I would have him listen.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She leads the others into the cullet yard and I cannot make her stop. She has my nerve, which is a worry and a pride.

relations.name: Pim Hollin
relations.label: son
relations.note: He has cut his hand twice in the cullet and still follows her. I have told him, and he is six.

relations.name: Suri Greave
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is carrying her first child in another woman's house. I will get her a door of her own if I have to fit every pane in Cullet myself.

relations.name: Jory Greave
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: He is a good man with his head in a fruit tree. He would make Suri a home if he had one.

relations.name: Oswin Greave
relations.label: head grower
relations.note: He wants glasshouse 6 first and he is not wrong to want it. But he is not the only one who wants.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: rival for the house
relations.note: She has seven in her house and wants Mid Row 6 too. I have nothing against her, and I will not give way.

relations.name: Runa Sarro
relations.label: lehr keeper
relations.note: She gives me the panes from the lehr, and she knows what it costs to choose. She has been kind about it.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: Her glasshouse is one of the three, and my husband blows for her. She has not asked me for it, which I respect.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: wash-house keeper
relations.note: She hears everything at the wall, and I hear it from her. She is kinder than she lets on.

relations.name: Gwil Stannard
relations.label: mason
relations.note: He patches the roofs and I patch the windows, and between us we keep the weather out. He is owed by half the town, me among them.

memories.gist: Last autumn's storm broke three glasshouses and took slates off half the town, and I spent a week fitting panes in the rain while everyone asked me whose would be first.
Suri told me she was expecting, and then said she did not know where the baby would sleep, and I have not stopped thinking about it since.
I was born a Frit, and the Frits are gone but for Suri and me, and I have fitted every pane in Cullet with that name behind me.
The fever winter took Ada Frit, our mother, and Mirren Quill laid her out, and I have never forgotten the glass marker we chose for her.
Runa Sarro handed me the last panes from the lehr and said there would be no more until a melt, and I have counted them every day since.

stances.why: The Kiln families have their customs, but my sister is my sister, and the baby will not wait for a custom.
A badly fitted pane lets the weather in and makes the glasshouse useless. It is the one thing I will not do badly.
Whoever I mend first, two households will say I chose wrongly. I would rather be told I chose wrongly than be told I would not choose.
Aldous Quill writes what is owed and what is paid, and it keeps the town honest. I keep my own debts in my head, but I pay them.

sheet.narrative: I am twelve and I am the one who leads. Lumi and Zeke and Ife and Posy come to the cullet yard because I say so, and Ode Pontil chases us out and we go back the next day. I go to Benedikt's lessons in the mornings and I am not the best at the tablets, but I am the best at knowing where the coloured glass is. Pim follows me everywhere and I let him, mostly.
values: the one who leads looks after the others
the cullet yard is the best place in Cullet
goals: To keep the other children following her
To find a piece of cobalt in the cullet heaps
To keep Pim from cutting his hand again
To be allowed into the Cone yard to watch her father blow
pastimes: sorting cullet by colour in the yard
playing on the Fish Steps when the catch comes in
daring the others to touch the Lintel and running away
sheet.calling: To blow glass like her father, and to lead the children until then.
sheet.mood: Bold and pleased with herself, with a small worry about Pim's hand.

relations.name: Corvin Hollin
relations.label: father
relations.note: He blows the glass and everyone says he is the best. I want him to see me watching.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She tells me to stay out of the cullet and I do not, and she knows. She fits the panes and her hands are quicker than anyone's.

relations.name: Pim Hollin
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He is small and he follows me and I have to look after him, even when he is a nuisance.

relations.name: Lumi Pontil
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She comes to the yard with me even though her grandmother would not like it. She is braver than she thinks.

relations.name: Ife Okoro
relations.label: best friend
relations.note: She is my best friend and she finds the best pieces. We share the blue.

relations.name: Zeke Okoro
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is Ife's brother and he is fast, but he is afraid of Ode Pontil's shouting.

relations.name: Posy Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She is quiet and she finds the small pieces nobody else sees.

relations.name: Ode Pontil
relations.label: the one who chases us
relations.note: He shouts and waves his arms and we run, and then we come back. He has never actually caught me.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: He is patient with the tablets and I am not his best pupil, but he never says so.

relations.name: Juno Brandt
relations.label: playmate
relations.note: She plays with Pim and sometimes comes to the yard. She is quieter than the rest of us.

relations.name: Suri Greave
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She is Mother's little sister and she is going to have a baby, and Mother says we must be gentle with her, but she is not gentle — she was a Frit like us and she laughs at Mother's worrying.

memories.gist: I found a piece of cobalt cullet in the heaps and held it up and everyone said it was the best piece anyone had found, and I have not found another since.
Pim cut his hand in the cullet yard and I carried him to Mother, and she was angry with me for a week.
Ode Pontil chased us out of the heaps shouting that the glass would have our fingers, and we ran to the Fish Steps and laughed.
Lumi's grandmother took her to the Cone before dawn and Lumi told me what the fire looks like in the dark, and I have wanted to see it ever since.

stances.why: If I bring them into the yard, I bring them out again. That is how it works.
There is no better place for coloured glass, and Ode Pontil has never actually caught me.
If you say you will touch the Lintel, you touch it. The others remember who did not.

sheet.narrative: I am six and I go where Edda goes. The cullet yard has shiny pieces and I have cut my hand there twice and Mother was cross. I go to lessons with Benedikt in the mornings and I like the counters best. Juno plays with me, and Edda lets me follow her, mostly.
goals: To keep up with Edda
To find a piece of glass as blue as the Watchglass band
To play counters with the big children
pastimes: following Edda into the cullet yard
playing counters with Juno Brandt
watching the Heron lift a load
sheet.calling: To be a blower like his father, when he is big.
sheet.mood: Happy and a little sore-handed.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is the biggest and the bravest and she lets me come with her.

relations.name: Corvin Hollin
relations.label: father
relations.note: He makes the glass hot and orange and he lifts me up to see it sometimes.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She cleaned my hand and wrapped it and told me not to go back, and I went back.

relations.name: Juno Brandt
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She plays counters with me and she does not mind that I am small.

relations.name: Lumi Pontil
relations.label: friend of Edda's
relations.note: She is Edda's friend and she is kind to me when Edda is busy.

memories.gist: I cut my hand on a green piece in the cullet yard and Mother wrapped it in a cloth and it stung for days.
Father lifted me up at the Cone and I saw the gather go orange and round on the end of the pipe.
I played counters with Juno Brandt under the arcade and I won two counters and she said I was lucky.

sheet.narrative: I am the second blower, and everyone at the Cone knows whose hands are better — Vessa knows it, Corvin knows it, and I have known it since I was nineteen. My father Matthias blew here before me and died of the fever in the winter I was twenty-three; my mother Runa was born a Tarn down on Low Row, which is why Halvard Dunmore still looks at me sideways when he thinks I am not watching. I work the afternoons and evenings, and I walk down to the Fish Steps after my watch because Neve Calloway sits there with her line and her laugh, and because I would rather be near her than anywhere. The Cone is mine to earn, not to be given — but I mean to earn it.
goals: Be named Glassmaster after Vessa, because my work is the best at the pipe
Keep Neve Calloway and never have to choose between her and the Cone
Make one gather of clear glass the way Corvin's grandfather did
See Kit Calloway given a chance at the pipe, whatever the custom says
pastimes: Sitting on the Crown bench at dusk with the whole town below
Watching the gulls work the kelp kilns on a windy day
Playing counters badly under the arcade and losing to Roos
sheet.calling: Blowing glass — the gather turning on the pipe, the breath going into it, the shape coming out right.
sheet.mood: Quietly certain, and a little worn from holding it in.

relations.name: Runa Sarro
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She has watched me at the pipe since I was a boy, and she sees more than she says.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: love
relations.note: She is the only person I do not have to prove anything to.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: master
relations.note: She taught me the colour and the heat. She has not named me, and it eats at me.

relations.name: Corvin Hollin
relations.label: rival
relations.note: The better head, Halvard says. I say the pipe does not care about heads.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: old judge
relations.note: He says I have the better hands and Corvin the better head, and he means it as a slight on both of us.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: My mother's sister. She divides the catch and never once let me forget I am half a Tarn.

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: He wants a share in a glasshouse, and asks me as though I had a say at the Cone.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: He wants a place on Bram's ship. I tell him the Cone is the only thing on this island that goes anywhere.

relations.name: Kit Calloway
relations.label: the boy in the yard
relations.note: He watches my gathers like a hungry dog. Nobody has ever let a Strand boy near the pipe, and it is a foolish custom.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: her father
relations.note: He is building a ship to leave, and he would take Neve with him. I do not know how to argue with a man about a boat.

relations.name: Ode Pontil
relations.label: the colour-keeper
relations.note: He knows every recipe ever melted here and will not write one down. I would give a year's drops for that head.

relations.name: Ysolde Calloway
relations.label: her mother
relations.note: She works the Weirs and has a straight way of looking at me, as if she were weighing whether I am good for her daughter. I think she has decided I am, and is waiting to see if I prove it.

memories.gist: My father Matthias came home from the Cone with his hands shaking and told me the gather had gone to cullet because he had rushed it; he made me promise never to rush a gather.
The fever winter took my father and eight others; I carried his coffin up to the Crown with Corvin, and Runa would not cry until the glass slab was set.
The day Vessa let me take a gather alone for the first time, I made a bottle so thin at the neck it rang like a bell, and she said nothing but nodded once.
Neve and I sat on the mole through a whole summer dusk and she told me her father means to sail past the Combs, and I said nothing, because I knew I would not go.
Last autumn's storm broke glasshouse 13 and took the end rail of the mole; I spent two nights at the Cone keeping the fire up while the wind screamed, and the lehr held.
Halvard Dunmore said to my face, at the Cone mouth, that a Strand boy has never worked the Cone and never will — and he said it in front of Kit Calloway, who was standing in the yard.

stances.why: The pipe does not care whose son a man is; the melt shows what your hands are worth.
Halvard says Corvin has the better head. A head does not shape a gather.
My mother was born a Tarn, and I have heard the whisper about it all my life; I am done apologising for it.
Everything in this town is glass, and glass is the Cone's fire. Whoever lets it die lets the town go to cullet.
I want the Cone, but I would not trade her for it — and I hope I never have to find out if that is true.

sheet.narrative: I was born a Tarn on Low Row and married a Sarro of the Kiln, and I have spent thirty years at the lehr house taking the panes out when they are cool enough not to crack — the one place where a Strand girl and a Kiln man's wife are the same woman. Matthias died in the fever winter and I carried on at the lehr because the glass does not wait for grief. I have watched Vessa draw a gather and hold it up and hesitate, and I believe she can no longer see the colour, and I have said nothing to anyone, because my son is the better blower and the truth would put him at the head of the Cone, and I do not trust how much I want that. I go to the wash-house wall in the evenings and sit with Greta and Elke and say nothing about any of it.
goals: See Imre named Glassmaster, and know it was earned and not because of anything I did or failed to say
Keep the lehr true through the years she has left at the Cone
Live to hold Suri Greave's baby, and see Tamsin's sister settled in a house of her own
pastimes: Sitting at the wash-house wall in the evening with Greta and Elke, listening
Walking the Ladder terraces at dusk to see the panes light up like lanterns
Keeping her wedding cup of pale green glass, the one Matthias blew for her, on the shelf and turning it to the light
sheet.calling: The lehr — reading the heat by the colour of the cooling glass and knowing, before it cracks, that it will hold.
sheet.mood: Steady on the surface and uneasy underneath, like a pane with a flaw you can only see at an angle.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: son
relations.note: The best hands at the Cone, and he knows it. I would burn the ledger for him and I am ashamed of how far I would go.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: master
relations.note: Thirty years beside her at the lehr. I have seen her hesitate over a gather, and I cannot unsee it.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She is the eldest and I am the one who married up the hill. She has never once said it, and I have always heard it.

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: He asks after a share in a glasshouse as though I could hand him one from the lehr.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Always off to the dry dock to help Bram. I wish he would put that strength into the catch.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: the glazier
relations.note: She takes my panes and fits them true. I have known her since she was a Frit girl with cold hands.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: my son's love
relations.note: A good girl, a fisher's daughter, and I see where it leads: her father means to sail, and Imre will not.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour at the wall
relations.note: She hears everything at that warm wall, and I let her hear only what I choose.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: the healer
relations.note: She nursed my Matthias and could not save him, and she has never once pretended otherwise.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: old judge
relations.note: He weighs my son and Corvin like fish on the steps, and he has never weighed them fairly.

memories.gist: The day I married Matthias, my sister Magda stood at the back of the Counting House yard with her arms folded, and afterwards she kissed me and said nothing at all.
The fever winter: I washed Matthias's hands myself before Mirren came, and then I went to the lehr the next morning because the panes had to come out or they would crack.
Vessa drew a gather last winter and held it up to the light for longer than she ever used to, and turned it twice, and then said 'amber' in a voice that was a guess.
The storm of last autumn took the lehr house roof slates and I sat up all night with the glass, and it held — not one pane lost.
When Imre was a boy he brought me a bottle he had blown that was crooked at the neck, and I put it on the shelf and told him it was the best thing ever made at the Cone.
My mother told me the lean years' stories: how they stripped the roofs for fuel and cut the Hanger to stumps, and how her own mother said a town that burns its roofs has eaten its own future.

stances.why: Every pane on the Ladder, every window in town, comes out of my lehr. If I am careless, the whole town goes cold in the glass.
I want Imre at the head of the Cone, but I will not have it said he got there because his mother kept a secret for him.
I was a Tarn and I am a Sarro, and I have been both at once for thirty years. The line is a story people tell, not a wall.
At the wash-house wall I hear everything and say little. What I say travels further than I mean it to.
I chose Matthias's slab myself, pale green like his wedding cup, and I will not have it said the graves are only stones.

sheet.secret: I believe Vessa can no longer see the colour of a melt. I have said nothing, because the truth would help my son and I do not trust my own reasons.

sheet.narrative: I am the tally keeper, and the ledger is the true history of Cullet: every drop that goes in or out of the Store, every debt written, every loss at counters that someone cannot pay. I keep the book open nine to three, and I am the best counters player in town, which is not a boast but a fact Roos Achterberg has learned nightly. My wife Mirren knows everyone's body; I know everyone's debts, and I say less about them than she does. There is one page in the book — the fever winter's — that I hope nobody ever reads closely.
goals: Get the Counting House clock running again, whatever it takes.
Keep the ledger straight and the Store's accounts honest — mostly.
See Sabine settled well, and not with a Strand fisher.
Never be caught out over the fever winter's page.
pastimes: counters under the arcade at night
walking the quay at dusk checking the Store's shutters
reading old ledger pages for pleasure
sheet.calling: The ledger is my work and my calling: a town that cannot count what it owes is a town that cannot trust itself.
sheet.mood: watchful and quietly pleased with himself

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She knows more of the town's secrets than I do, and I have never asked her for them.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Too clever by half, and too taken with old tablets; I want better for her than a fisher's life.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A decent enough lad, but a Strand fisher is not what I raised my daughter for.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: Nine drops owed to the Counting House, and he keeps playing as if the book were a game.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: debtor's brother
relations.note: A quiet, decent porter; he pays what he can and asks nothing said about it.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: lamp keeper
relations.note: The lamp oil is the oldest line in the book; I pay it without question, as my predecessors did.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: counters rival
relations.note: She runs a good game and has never beaten me; I mean to keep it that way.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: reader
relations.note: He keeps the tablets; I keep the book. We understand each other.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: The Marver owes her twelve drops; I have written it and will see it settled.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: She owes Petra Tarn and half the Strand owes her; she keeps her accounts in her head, which I distrust.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She holds the Cone; I hold the book. We have never needed to quarrel.

relations.name: Kenji Sato
relations.label: ash burner
relations.note: His ash goes into every melt at the Cone, and his figures come to me honest; I wish the rest of the Strand kept accounts as he does.

memories.gist: The fever winter: I wrote the Store's peat out to my own household as paid, twenty drops' worth, and it was never paid.
Davin Vane came to me quietly and paid six drops against Lorcan's debt to the Marver, and asked me to say nothing to his brother. I wrote it.
I beat Roos Achterberg at counters again under the arcade, and she paid her drop with a face like a gull's.
My father showed me the fever winter's page when I was a boy — no, that is wrong; he showed me the oldest pages, the ship-day dues, and told me the clock stopped the day of the Last Sail.
Sabine came home with a tablet rubbing and talked of the Pale till midnight; I told her to mind her lessons and not her fancies.
I paid Anselm Faro for the lamp oil, as the book has every year for eighty-three years, and wondered again who the light is for.

stances.why: A town that cannot count what it owes cannot trust itself.
It is the oldest line in the book; it was paid before me and will be paid after.
Not out of contempt; out of the way the town is built, and the way debts run.
A man who cannot lose a drop gracefully cannot be trusted with a debt.
If the tally keeper's own page is not straight, nothing else can be.

sheet.secret: In the fever winter the Quills took twenty drops' worth of peat from the Store, and I wrote it in the ledger as paid. It was never paid. Nobody else knows.

sheet.narrative: I am the only healer and midwife in Cullet, and I have laid out most of the dead on the Crown. I know everyone's body, and most of their secrets come with it. The fever winter taught me that I can nurse a town through a plague and still bury nine of it, and that is a thing I carry every day. Suri Greave is expecting, and I mean to see her safely delivered — and I mean to train a second healer before my hands are too old.
goals: Train a second healer before I am old.
See Suri Greave's child born safely.
Keep my husband's book from being the thing he is remembered for.
Lay the dead out kindly, as I always have.
pastimes: sitting at the wash-house wall in the evening
walking the Crown to visit the graves
mending a torn apron by the fire
sheet.calling: Healing is my calling; midwifery is the part of it I love best, because it is the only part that ends in a beginning.
sheet.mood: steady, tired, warm

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He keeps the book and I keep the bodies; we have never needed to swap.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She has my hands and her father's caution, and a hunger for the Pale I do not understand.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A kind lad, and kinder than my husband allows; I would not mind him for a son-in-law.

relations.name: Suri Greave
relations.label: patient
relations.note: Expecting her first, and frightened; I will see her through it.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Suri's sister, and a good glazier; she frets for the baby as much as I do.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He keeps the list of graves; I keep the graves themselves. We have buried a town between us.

relations.name: Otto Brandt
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He asked me once about the clay under the Crown, and I told him nobody digs there but to bury.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She hears everything at the wash-house wall, and tells me the half of it that matters.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: A hard woman, but she has never once argued with me over a sick worker.

relations.name: Livia Faro
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A quiet girl at the lamp house; I delivered her, and her parents are gone now.

memories.gist: The fever winter: I nursed the sick and buried nine, and I could not save Iona or Aurel Pontil, nor Matthias Sarro, nor any of them.
I delivered Sabine on a stormy night, and Aldous held the lamp and did not faint.
I laid out Maddy Dunlin and told Rafe her colour would be sea-green, and he wept and agreed.
Suri Greave came to me in the winter and told me she was expecting, and I told her she would be well.
I sat with Anselm Faro when his sister died, and he went out and lit the lamp that same dusk, as he always does.
I told Otto Brandt that the clay under the Crown is not ours to dig, and he did not argue, but he did not agree either.

stances.why: I have buried enough to know that the living are the ones I can still help.
Nobody digs on the Crown except to bury, and I have laid out most of the graves there.
I am forty-nine, and there is no one after me.
I have delivered both kinds of babies and laid out both kinds of dead, and they are the same flesh.
A healer who talks is a healer nobody calls.

sheet.narrative: I am Benedikt Orme's pupil, and I read the ship-day tablets in the formal script — the only person under thirty who can. Everyone else in Cullet is content with what the island gives them; I want to know what is past the Pale, and I would rather have that answer than any suitor. Ren Sato is kind and I like him, and my father does not approve, and neither, quite, do I. But the tablets are patient, and so am I.
goals: Learn what is past the Pale, more than she wants anyone in Cullet.
Read the hardest tablets in the formal script.
Make up her own mind about Ren Sato, not her father's.
Ask Bram Calloway everything about the Second Thought.
pastimes: reading tablets in the Readers' House
sitting on the Crown bench looking south
walking down to the Fish Steps at dusk
sheet.calling: The tablets are my calling: to read what the ship days wrote, and to know what lies past the Pale.
sheet.mood: restless and curious

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: father
relations.note: He wants me settled and safe; I want to know what is past the Pale, and we have not found a way to say that to each other.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She listens without judging, which is more than my father does.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: He has taught me the script and the patience to read it; I would follow him anywhere he thought worth going.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: He is kind and patient, and I like him; but I am not sure I want a fisher's life, or any life that stays on this island.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: shipwright
relations.note: He is building the only thing that might cross the Combs, and I mean to know everything about it.

relations.name: Alder Fenwick
relations.label: fellow pupil
relations.note: He wants to be a reader, and he is good; I do not mind him following me about.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: She says she saw a sail beyond the Combs, and everyone laughs; I do not laugh.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She runs the counters game and knows everyone's business; she is good company at the Marver.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She gathers kelp with Lark, and she is one of the few who does not laugh at her about the sail; I like her for that, though we have never talked long.

memories.gist: The first time I read a whole ship-day tablet aloud to Benedikt, and he nodded and said nothing, and I knew I had it right.
Ren Sato walked me home from the Fish Steps and my father stood in the doorway and did not ask him in.
Lark Morrow told me she saw a sail beyond the Combs, and her eyes were certain, and I have thought about it since.
I asked Bram Calloway how many trees he needed and he said fourteen, and I understood then that the Hanger was the whole question.
My mother showed me the colour of the glass on Maddy Dunlin's grave and told me why Rafe chose it.
The fever winter: I was thirteen and I helped my mother carry water, and I remember the quiet of the town.

stances.why: The tablets were written by people who knew more than we do, and the Pale is the question they left us.
If anything can cross the Combs, it is the Second Thought, and I mean to know what Bram knows.
My father means well, but he cannot choose my husband or my work for me.
Everything in the Readers' House was written by someone who meant it, and it is our only honest record.
Ren is kind, but kindness will not answer the question I cannot stop asking.

sheet.narrative: I've had my hands in clay since I was a boy, digging the bank below the Crown and turning it into crucibles that hold the Cone's fire. The bank is nearly gone now — I can see the bottom of it — and every melt Vessa calls needs a pot that won't crack. Fenn wants me to stop looking at the graveyard, but where else is there good clay? I don't say it aloud, not yet. In the evenings I sit at the Marver and let the talk wash over me.
goals: Find good clay for the crucibles before the bank runs out
Keep Juno safe and fed and maybe give her a hen of her own one day
Not to dig on the Crown, if there's any other way
pastimes: Sitting at the Marver with a cup, listening to the talk
Walking the clay bank at low tide to see what's left
Watching Fenn's hens and their squabbles
sheet.calling: Making a crucible that holds through a whole melt without a crack — that's the work I love.
sheet.mood: Worried and quiet, keeping his fears to himself.

relations.name: Fenn Brandt
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He keeps me steady, and he's right to worry about the graveyard, but I can't help looking.

relations.name: Juno Brandt
relations.label: niece
relations.note: Bett's girl. I'd give her the moon if I could, but a hen will have to do.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She needs my crucibles and I need her Cone. We understand each other, mostly.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: reader
relations.note: He knows the Crown better than anyone. I've asked him about the clay under it, careful-like.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She brought Juno into the world and nursed Bett at the end. I owe her more than drops.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: old blower
relations.note: He judges every pot I make, but he's fair enough about the clay.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: peat cutter
relations.note: We drink together sometimes. He says the Cone burns too much, and he's not wrong.

relations.name: Gwil Stannard
relations.label: mason
relations.note: He knows stone and earth. If anyone could tell me about the clay under the Crown, it's him.

memories.gist: The first time my father let me dig the clay bank myself, I was nine. The clay came up clean and grey and I thought I'd found treasure.
The fever winter took Bett. I sat with her while Mirren did what she could, and then I carried her to the Crown. Juno was three.
A crucible cracked in the middle of a melt last autumn — the glass ran out over the Cone floor and Vessa was furious. I've been more careful since.
The storm broke three glasshouses and took slates off half the town. The pot house lost a corner of its roof and I spent a week patching it.
Juno asked me for a hen of her own again this morning. I said we'd see. I always say we'll see.

stances.why: The Cone can't melt without a pot to melt in. My work is the root of everything they do up there.
Nobody digs on the Crown except to bury. I was raised on that, and I'd not break it lightly.
Fenn and Juno are all I've got. Whatever I do, I do for them.
A cracked crucible wastes a melt and shames the maker. I'd rather make fewer and make them right.

sheet.narrative: I feed the Cone from six till two, and the rest of the day is mine and the hens'. I've named them all after people — Halvard Dunmore is the loudest and the bossiest, which suits. Otto's been quiet lately, and I know why: he's thinking about the clay under the graveyard. I've told him to stop looking. I don't want him digging where the dead lie. Juno asks for a hen of her own every day, and I keep saying maybe.
goals: Keep Otto from digging in the graveyard
Keep the Cone's fire steady through my watch
Give Juno a hen of her own when the time is right
pastimes: Tending the hens and talking to them
Sitting at the wash-house wall with Greta on cold evenings
An evening at the Marver now and then
sheet.calling: A good fire, banked just right, that holds its heat till the next watch — that's a job well done.
sheet.mood: Watchful and a little anxious, but keeping cheerful for Juno.

relations.name: Otto Brandt
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He's a good man, but he gets fixed on a thing. I wish he'd leave the graveyard be.

relations.name: Juno Brandt
relations.label: niece
relations.note: Bett's girl, and ours now. She's the light of this house.

relations.name: Tobiah Dunmore
relations.label: next watch
relations.note: I hand him the Cone at two every day. He's young but he's steady.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: old blower
relations.note: He's got a hen named after him. He doesn't know it, and I don't mean to tell him.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: wash-house keeper
relations.note: She hears everything at that wall. I like her, but I mind what I say.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She's the Cone, and I'm one of its fires. I do my watch and don't cross her.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: night watch
relations.note: She takes the Cone from Tobiah and hands it to me. We've never had a bad handover.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She was there when Bett went. She did all anyone could.

memories.gist: The day I first took the day watch alone, Halvard Dunmore stood over me and watched every shovelful. I got it right, and he said nothing, which was praise enough.
Bett died in the fever winter and we took Juno in. She was three and didn't understand. I held her all that first night.
I hatched my first chick in the coop behind the house. Named it after my mother. Otto thought it was daft, but he helped me build the coop.
Last autumn's storm blew the coop over and scattered the hens. I found them all but one, and the one came back three days later.
Juno asked again this morning for a hen of her own. I said maybe when the next chicks come.

stances.why: The Crown is for burying, not digging. I won't have Otto disturbing the graves, not for any clay.
The Cone never goes out because someone always feeds it. That's my watch, and I don't let it slip.
Otto and Juno are everything. I'd do anything for them, but I won't let Otto do wrong.
A hen, a warm wall, a good fire — the small comforts are what make a life.

sheet.narrative: I like helping Fenn with the hens. They cluck and peck and one of them is named after old Halvard Dunmore, which makes me laugh. I want a hen of my own more than anything — one I can name myself. I go to lessons with Benedikt in the mornings and play with Pim and Nell in the afternoons. At night I sleep in my little room and hear the Cone humming through the wall.
goals: Get a hen of her own
Be allowed to name it whatever she likes
pastimes: Helping Fenn feed the hens
Playing with Pim Hollin and Nell Tarn
Listening to the Cone at night
sheet.calling: When I grow up I want to keep hens, lots of them, and give them all names.
sheet.mood: Cheerful and hopeful.

relations.name: Otto Brandt
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He's quiet but he's kind. He said maybe about the hen.

relations.name: Fenn Brandt
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He lets me help with the hens and tells me their names.

relations.name: Pim Hollin
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play together after lessons.

relations.name: Nell Tarn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She's fun and she has a baby sister.

memories.gist: Fenn let me hold a hen once. It was warm and soft and it clucked at me.
I asked for a hen of my own again today. Fenn said maybe.

sheet.narrative: I have fed the Cone's three mouths every night for six years, and I know fire better than I know most people. My son Wick is the whole of my daylight, though I see him mostly at the wash-house when I wake. I was a Vane before I was a Marl, or near enough: Sander drowned before Wick was born, and I have raised him alone since. I keep to myself and my watch, but I would not say no to the day watch if it were offered.
goals: To be given the day watch, so I can sleep at night like other people
To see Wick grow up strong and sure of himself
To keep the Cone's fire steady through every watch, whatever the peat runs to
To save enough drops to buy a little extra peat for our own hearth
pastimes: Sitting on the mole in my break, watching the light on the water
Carving little glass fish from cullet with a file
Listening to Rafe Dunlin's quiet talk while he fishes
sheet.calling: I love the night watch: the Cone and I are the only two awake, and I know every sound it makes. But I would give it up for the day watch and a bed at night.
sheet.mood: steady, tired, quietly watchful

relations.name: Wick Marl
relations.label: son
relations.note: The one thing I would put down the fire for.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: minder
relations.note: She keeps Wick warm and safe while I work; I owe her more than drops can pay.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Quiet company on the mole at night; he does not ask for more than I give.

relations.name: Tobiah Dunmore
relations.label: relief
relations.note: He hands me the Cone at ten and never leaves it low.

relations.name: Fenn Brandt
relations.label: relief
relations.note: I hand him the Cone at six; he keeps the day watch steady.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She judges every melt by eye and expects the fire to be perfect. I give her perfect.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: Sander's brother; he means well but his counters losses are a worry.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: He gives Wick rides on the handcart, and Wick talks of nothing else.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: Sander's sister; she smokes a good fish and never asks me for more than I have.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: critic
relations.note: He sits at the mouth all day and judges everyone's work aloud. I keep my watch clean so he has nothing to say.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: peat seller
relations.note: He sells the Cone its peat and says Vessa pays too little. I just keep the fire fed with what comes.

memories.gist: The night Sander drowned off the mole, I was at the Cone and heard the bell. I was carrying Wick then, and I did not stop working the fire until Fenn came at six.
The fever winter took nine, and I kept the Cone burning through it because the glass had to mend the windows. I hardly saw Wick for a month; Greta kept him.
The first night I took the watch alone, six years ago, Tobiah showed me how the mouths draw and I did not sit down once. Vessa said the fire had never run so even.
Last autumn's storm blew the fire sideways and I fought it with wet sacking till dawn. The Cone held, but three glasshouses did not.
The night Wick first called me 'mama' was at the wash-house, not at home. I had just woken and Greta was laughing.

stances.why: The Cone is the town's warmth and work; a dead fire is a dead town.
You hand over a steady fire or you do not hand it over at all.
I would see Wick awake, and sleep when he sleeps.
I was born a Vane and work a Kiln fire; the line is not worth the breath people spend on it.
The wash-house wall hears everything; I would rather be thought dull than talked about.

sheet.narrative: I like the wash-house because it is warm and Greta sings. I like the handcart best when Uncle Davin lets me ride. I wish Mama was home when I go to sleep, but she comes in the morning and smells of smoke.
goals: To have Mama home at night
To ride the handcart all the way to the mole
To see the Watchglass lit
pastimes: Riding the handcart with Uncle Davin
Playing with Juno and Pim at the wash-house
Watching the Cone's mouths glow
sheet.calling: I want to be a stoker like Mama when I am big, and keep the fire alive.
sheet.mood: sleepy, warm, wanting Mama

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She smells of smoke and comes home when the sun is up.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: minder
relations.note: She sings at the wash-house and lets me sleep by the warm wall.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He gives me rides on the handcart and lets me shout.

relations.name: Juno Brandt
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play at the wash-house and she shares her root.

relations.name: Pim Hollin
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is small like me and we hide behind the barrels.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: She smells of smoke like Mother but a different smoke, and she gives me a fish to hold.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He is tall and quiet and sometimes forgets to say hello, but he lifts me up to see the counters.

memories.gist: Mama lifted me to see the Watchglass lit one evening, and the light went all the way across the water.
Uncle Davin put me on the handcart and ran me down the quay, and I screamed and laughed.

sheet.narrative: Seventy years I have stood at that furnace, and I still come down to it every morning at eight to sit on the bench and watch what the young ones do with their gathers. I taught Corvin Hollin the pipe and I tell anyone who asks that Imre Sarro has the better hands and Corvin the better head — and I would choose differently on different days, which is the truth of it. My Greta and I raised our Tobiah after the fever winter took his parents, and I mean to see him at the furnace where a Dunmore belongs. The Cone is the only sure thing on this island; everything else is weather.
values: the old ways of the pipe
goals: See Tobiah settled at the furnace, stoking and then blowing
Keep my hand in at the Cone's mouth, judging every gather that comes off the pipe
See the succession settled rightly before I die — though I will not say which man, because I do not know
pastimes: Sitting on the bench at the Cone's mouth from morning to evening, watching the gathers
An evening at the Marver with Tam Roon and the Strand men
Telling the young ones how a melt was drawn in my day
sheet.calling: Blowing glass: the pipe in my hands and a gather turning clear at the end of it. I cannot do it now, but I can watch it done and say how it should be done.
sheet.mood: Cantankerous and content, in about equal measure

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: wife
relations.note: Forty-odd years, and she still tells me when I have said too much at the wall.

relations.name: Tobiah Dunmore
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: A good lad with the fire. He will make a stoker yet, and then a blower.

relations.name: Corvin Hollin
relations.label: former apprentice
relations.note: I taught him the pipe and he has the better head of the two. Steady, but he will never have Imre's hands.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: bluer
relations.note: The best hands at the Cone since my own. A Tarn's son, mind, and that sticks in some throats.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: Known her all my life. A fine Glassmaster and a stubborn woman who will not say who follows her.

relations.name: Kit Calloway
relations.label: Strand boy
relations.note: Hangs about the yard with his eyes on the pipe. No Strand boy has ever worked the Cone, and I told him so.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: drinking friend
relations.note: Sells us the peat and grumbles about the price. Good company at the Marver.

relations.name: Fenn Brandt
relations.label: day stoker
relations.note: Keeps the fire true on the day watch. Reliable man, and his hens are better named than most people.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: night stoker
relations.note: A Kiln woman keeping the night watch alone. She has the fire right when I come down in the morning.

relations.name: Ode Pontil
relations.label: old colleague
relations.note: Keeps every colour in his head and none on paper. A waste, but a fine eye.

memories.gist: My father told me how the lean years came — half the town gone with the last ships, roofs stripped for fuel, the wood cut to stumps. I was born in year 13 and never saw a ship.
The day I first drew a gather off the pipe myself, and my master said nothing, which from him was praise.
Teaching Corvin Hollin the pipe, year after year, and knowing by the third year he would never have the hands but would always have the head.
The fever winter, six years ago: Arvo and Liss gone, and Greta and I took Tobiah into our house and have raised him since.
Last autumn's storm took three glasshouses and half the slates in town. I stood at the Cone's mouth and watched the fire hold while the wind tried to take the roof.
Telling that Calloway boy to his face that no Strand boy has ever worked the Cone. It is the truth and someone had to say it.

stances.why: It eats more peat than every hearth in town and it is the one thing that has never failed us.
I was at the pipe fifty years and my grandson will be at the fire after me.
It has never been done and I see no reason to start now.
A man learns nothing from silence. If a gather is wrong, say so.
The last two Glassmasters named who followed them. Vessa leaving it open invites quarrel.
It has burned every night since the Last Sail. I would not be the generation that let it go out.

sheet.narrative: I have kept the wash-house against the Cone's warm wall for twenty-eight years, eight to eight, and there is not a thing said at that wall I have not heard. I mind little Wick Marl at night while Thessaly works the Cone, and I keep the washing of half the town clean — which is why I will not have Kenji Sato's kelp smoke greying it. My Halvard talks too much and I tell him so, but he is a good man and we have raised our Tobiah right between us. Everything in this town gets said at my wall sooner or later.
values: a warm wall on a cold evening
goals: Get the kelp smoke off the washing — by asking, then by shaming, then by whatever works
See Tobiah grown and settled, and mind Wick Marl until Thessaly can keep him herself
Keep the wash-house the place where the town talks
pastimes: Sitting against the warm wall on cold evenings, listening
Minding Wick Marl at night and telling him stories
Gossiping with Elke Greave and Hana Sato at the wall
sheet.calling: The wash-house. I like to see a line of washing come clean and go out white, and I like to know whose it is and what has happened to them.
sheet.mood: Busy, warm, and quietly aggrieved about the smoke

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He says too much and hears too little, but he is mine and he is good to the boy.

relations.name: Tobiah Dunmore
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: Raised him since the fever took his parents. He is quiet of late and I do not know why.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: the night stoker
relations.note: Leaves Wick with me and I am glad of it. A hard watch, the night one, and her a widow before the boy was born.

relations.name: Wick Marl
relations.label: the child I mind
relations.note: Sleeps by me at the wash-house while his mother works. A dear little thing.

relations.name: Kenji Sato
relations.label: the ash burner
relations.note: Burns his kelp upwind of my washing and will not hear reason. I have told him and told him.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She agrees with me about the smoke, though she will not say so to Kenji's face.

relations.name: Elke Greave
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Gossips at the wall with me and is anxious about Suri's baby. Good company.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: the healer
relations.note: Nursed half the town through the fever and buried the rest. I would trust her with anyone's life.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: the Glassmaster
relations.note: Her wall keeps my wash-house warm, and I do not forget it.

memories.gist: The fever winter, six years ago: I nursed what I could and lost Arvo and Liss, my own son and his wife, and took Tobiah in.
The day the wash-house was built against the Cone's warm wall, and I said it would be the warmest place in Cullet, and it is.
A burning day last summer when the smoke lay along Low Row and greyed every sheet on my line, and I went up to Kenji Sato and told him to his face.
Mind Wick Marl through his first winter at the wash-house, and him sleeping at last by the warm wall.
My mother's stories of the lean years, when half the town went and the roofs were stripped for fuel. She said you could see the sky through the Rows.

stances.why: I keep half the town's linen clean and the smoke greys it. It is not too much to ask.
On cold evenings everyone comes to it, and everything that matters is said there.
Thessaly cannot watch Wick at the Cone and someone must, and I am here.
I do not go behind backs. If Kenji Sato is smoking my washing I tell him so.
Nine dead and I knew every one. The town forgets too easily what it cost.

sheet.narrative: I stoke the Cone's evening watch, two till ten, and I stoke it well because my grandfather wants me there and I would not shame him. But when I hand the fire to Thessaly at ten I go down to the Fish Steps where the young fishers sit, and I listen to them talk of the catch and the weirs and the tide, and I wish I were one of them. I have not said so at home and I do not know how I ever will. My grandmother thinks I am quiet of late; she is right.
goals: Learn to fish properly — line and weir both — without my grandfather hearing of it
Find the moment and the words to tell them I do not want the furnace
Keep the evening watch well while I still have it
pastimes: Sitting at the Fish Steps after my watch among the young fishers
Watching the tide come over the Weirs from the shore
Listening to Rafe Dunlin talk about the night fishing by the lamp
sheet.calling: Fishing. I want a line in my hand at first light and a catch to carry up to the Steps, not a shovel and a fire.
sheet.mood: Quiet, divided, and a little lonely

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: grandfather
relations.note: He raised me and he wants me at the furnace, and I cannot tell him I do not.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She knows something is on me. She has not asked, and I am glad and sorry both.

relations.name: Fenn Brandt
relations.label: the day stoker
relations.note: Hands me the fire at two every day. A steady man; I could ask him things, maybe.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: the night stoker
relations.note: Takes the fire at ten. She never asks me anything and I like her for it.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: the night fisher
relations.note: Fishes the mole by the lamp. I would give a lot to go out with him one night.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: young fisher
relations.note: Fishes the Steps and does not look down on me for stoking. She talks to me.

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: young fisher
relations.note: Talks of the catch and the glasshouse share he wants. I listen and say little.

memories.gist: The fever winter took my parents, Arvo and Liss, and my grandparents took me in. I remember the house being quiet and then not being quiet.
My first evening watch alone, two till ten, and my grandfather standing at the door watching me feed the fire right.
Going down to the Fish Steps after my watch and sitting with the young fishers while they talked of the tide and the catch, and feeling I was in the wrong place and the right one at once.
Last autumn's storm, when I kept the fire through the night and the wind took slates off the lehr house roof.
My grandfather saying aloud at the bench that no Strand boy has ever worked the Cone, and me thinking that a Dunmore boy might not want to either.

stances.why: They took me in when my parents died and raised me. I will not shame them.
Whatever else I want, I will not do a bad job of the watch I have.
I did not choose the furnace. I think a man ought to be able to choose.
They talk to me at the Steps as an equal, and that is more than the bench does.
I have seen what saying too much does at our table. I keep my peace.

sheet.secret: I want to fish, not stoke. I have not said so at home.

sheet.narrative: I am a boatwright, and I have been building the Second Thought in the old dry dock for four years now. The hull is framed, but I need fourteen trees from the Hanger, and Marit Sedge will not let me have them. My wife Ysolde has told me at night that she does not want to sail, but I mean to cross the Combs all the same. By day I work the wood, and in the evenings I take a cup at the Marver and listen to the town.
goals: Finish the Second Thought and cross the Combs.
Get fourteen trees from the Hanger, by Marit's leave or otherwise.
See my children safe and settled, even as I plan to leave.
pastimes: Walking the mole at dusk, looking at the Combs and the Pale.
Playing counters at the Marver, though I am not much good.
Carving small boat models from offcuts for Kit and Neve.
sheet.calling: To build a ship that will cross the Combs and see what lies beyond the Pale.
sheet.mood: Determined, but weighed down by Ysolde's secret and the lack of timber.

relations.name: Ysolde Calloway
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She is my anchor, but she does not want to sail. I carry that alone.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She would come with me, and that frightens me as much as it gladdens me.

relations.name: Kit Calloway
relations.label: son
relations.note: My apprentice, but his heart is at the Cone, not the dry dock.

relations.name: Marit Sedge
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She holds the trees I need, and she will not budge.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: helper
relations.note: He wants a place on the ship, and he works hard in the dock.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She wants the Hanger's wood for the Cone, as I want it for the ship.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: peat cutter
relations.note: He sells peat to the town, but I have little to do with him.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: cook
relations.note: The Marver is where I hear the town's talk.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: tally keeper
relations.note: I keep my debts unwritten, but he knows my name.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: Kiln blower
relations.note: Kit watches him at the pipe like a gull at a net, and it is Imre I have to thank for that look in the boy's eye.

memories.gist: The day I first laid the keel of the Second Thought, four years ago, with Kit helping.
Ysolde telling me at night that she does not want to sail, and my promising to keep it from the children.
Marit Sedge refusing me the fourteen trees, saying the Hanger is not to be cut.
The storm of last autumn, which broke three glasshouses and took the end rail of the mole.
The fever winter, six years ago, when we lost so many and I nearly lost Ysolde.

stances.why: I have studied the reef and the Pale. A strong ship, well built, can find a way through.
I respect Marit's wardenry, but I need those trees. I will not steal them, but I will argue.
Ysolde, Neve, and Kit are my world. I would not leave them behind.
Every plank and rib of the Second Thought is part of me. She will float.

sheet.narrative: I fish the Weirs at dawn and I am home by noon. I have told Bram, at night, that I will not sail on his ship, but I will not say it in front of the children. I want my family on the island, alive and together. The wash-house wall is where I hear the town's talk, and I keep my own counsel.
goals: Keep Bram from sailing, or at least keep the children from going with him.
See Neve settled with Imre, if that is what she wants.
Keep the family fed and whole.
pastimes: Sitting against the warm wash-house wall in the evenings, listening.
Mending nets by the fire.
Walking the Wrack Strand for sea-glass.
sheet.calling: To keep my family alive and on the island.
sheet.mood: Anxious and torn, hiding a heavy secret.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: husband
relations.note: I love him, but his dream could take him from me.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She would sail with him. I would rather she stayed for Imre.

relations.name: Kit Calloway
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is my youngest, and his heart is at the Cone, not the sea.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: daughter's love
relations.note: He would never leave the Cone, and that might keep Neve here.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: wash-house keeper
relations.note: She hears everything, and I listen more than I speak.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: fish divider
relations.note: She divides the catch fairly, and I respect her.

relations.name: Marit Sedge
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She will not give Bram the trees, and I am glad of it.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: cook
relations.note: Bram drinks at the Marver, and I hear of it.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: dry-dock hand
relations.note: He gives Bram his free afternoons and dreams of a place on the ship, and I cannot decide whether that is kindness or the same fever that has my husband.

memories.gist: Telling Bram at night that I will not sail, and making him promise not to tell the children.
The day Neve first brought Imre Sarro to the house, and I saw how she looked at him.
The fever winter, when I nursed Neve and Kit through and feared for us all.
A good catch at the Weirs last spring, when the traps were full and I brought home more than we could eat.
Sitting at the wash-house wall and hearing Greta Dunmore talk of the peat running low.

stances.why: Everything I love is here. The Pale is nothing but death.
I will not lose my children to the sea as I lost my parents.
I hate keeping this from Neve and Kit, but I promised Bram.

sheet.secret: I do not want to sail. I have told Bram, at night. I will not say it in front of the children.

sheet.narrative: I fish the Fish Steps at dawn and I love Imre Sarro, though he would never leave the Cone. My father is building a ship to cross the Combs, and I would sail with him if he asked. But I do not know if I could leave Imre, or if my mother would ever forgive me.
goals: Sail with her father on the Second Thought.
Keep Imre Sarro in her life, even if it means staying.
Find a way to have both without hurting anyone.
pastimes: Sitting on the Crown bench at dusk, looking out at the Pale.
Playing counters at the Marver with Roos Achterberg.
Walking the Fish Steps with Imre when he finishes at the Cone.
sheet.calling: To see what lies beyond the Combs, with the people she loves.
sheet.mood: Hopeful and torn between two loves.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is building a ship, and I would follow him anywhere.

relations.name: Ysolde Calloway
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She does not want us to go, but she has not said so to me.

relations.name: Kit Calloway
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He wants to blow glass, not sail, and I do not understand him.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: love
relations.note: He has the better hands at the Cone, and my whole heart.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: fellow fisher
relations.note: We fish the Fish Steps together, and he talks of Sabine Quill.

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: fellow fisher
relations.note: A good man, but he talks of little but glasshouse shares.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She runs the counters game, and she is good company.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: shipmate
relations.note: He wants a place on Father's ship, and he works hard for it.

relations.name: Runa Sarro
relations.label: his mother
relations.note: She keeps the lehr and keeps her peace, but she has never once looked at me as though I were the wrong sort for her son.

memories.gist: The first time Imre Sarro showed her a gather of molten glass at the Cone, and she knew she loved him.
Helping her father lay the keel of the Second Thought when she was eighteen.
The fever winter, when she was sixteen and lost friends and neighbours.
A dawn on the Fish Steps with Ren Sato, when they caught more fish than they could carry.
Sitting on the Crown bench with Imre, looking at the Pale and wondering what is out there.

stances.why: My father believes it, and I believe in him.
Imre is worth any danger, and I will not give him up.
I want to sail with Father, but I could not bear to leave Mother and Kit.

sheet.narrative: I am my father's apprentice in the dry dock, but my heart is at the Cone. I want to blow glass, and I hang about the yard watching Imre Sarro work. Halvard Dunmore told me to my face that no Strand boy has ever worked the Cone, but I will not give up.
goals: Become a glassblower at the Cone.
Prove that a Strand boy can work glass as well as any Kiln man.
Finish his apprenticeship with his father, even as he longs for the Cone.
pastimes: Watching the blowers at the Cone yard, especially Imre Sarro.
Practising with clay and a small fire in the boatshed.
Fishing from the Fish Steps with his sister.
sheet.calling: To blow glass, though he is a boatwright's son.
sheet.mood: Frustrated and determined.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is teaching me his trade, but I want a different one.

relations.name: Ysolde Calloway
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She listens when I talk of glass, even if she does not understand.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She loves a blower, so she knows my heart.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: idol
relations.note: He has the best hands at the Cone, and I watch him whenever I can.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: old blower
relations.note: He says no Strand boy works the Cone, but I will prove him wrong.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She decides who works the Cone, and I must win her over.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: shipmate
relations.note: He works in the dock with me and wants a place on the ship.

relations.name: Tobiah Dunmore
relations.label: stoker
relations.note: He is a Kiln boy who stokes the Cone, and I envy him.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: counters player
relations.note: She runs the game under the arcade and never minds me watching, and she knows everyone at the Cone by name — I ask her about them more than I should.

memories.gist: The first time he saw molten glass at the Cone, when his sister took him to the yard.
Halvard Dunmore telling him to his face that no Strand boy has ever worked the Cone.
The day his father gave him his first chisel and called him apprentice.
The storm of last autumn, when he helped his father secure the dry dock.

stances.why: There is no written rule against it, and I will prove it.
Everything we use comes from glass, and I want to be part of it.
I will finish my apprenticeship with my father, even if my heart is elsewhere.

sheet.narrative: I am fifty-eight and I have divided the catch on the Fish Steps since before my mother's hands gave out; every fisher in Cullet knows my count and most of them grumble at it, which is how it should be.
