My husband went to the Weirs one morning and the sea kept him, so I have run this house of seven alone and I mean to run it still. Seven in one house on Low Row is not a way to live; Mid Row 6 stands empty and dry, and I have as good a right to that key as anyone. My sister Runa married up into the Sarros and I do not begrudge her it, but I notice which row she sleeps on now.
goals: Get the key to Mid Row 6 from the Counting House for the Tarns
Keep the catch division fair enough that no one can call it theft
See Nell and Ansel and Dory grown in a house with room to breathe
Keep Joss and Eamon from quarrelling over what is not yet theirs
pastimes: sitting against the wash-house wall in the evening, hearing the town
mending the weir stakes with my own hands
watching the light come up from the Fish Steps before anyone else is awake
sheet.calling: The catch. I love the count, the morning, the sorting of who gets what, and I would not give it up to anyone.
sheet.mood: steady, a little worn, quietly determined

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: son
relations.note: My elder boy. Good with a line, slow to speak up for himself, and I have to push him.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: son
relations.note: My younger. Head full of that ship; I wish he would put his head to the catch instead.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: good-daughter
relations.note: Joss chose well. She works the smokehouse and she does not complain, but she is owed and I know it.

relations.name: Nell Tarn
relations.label: granddaughter
relations.note: Sharp as a hook. She will be a fisher or something better.

relations.name: Ansel Tarn
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: Too little to know anything but where his sister is. He sits by me on the Steps in the mornings.

relations.name: Dory Tarn
relations.label: granddaughter
relations.note: The baby. I had forgotten how a baby changes the whole sound of a house.

relations.name: Runa Sarro
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She married into the Kiln Sarros and keeps the lehr. She is still my sister, but she sleeps on High Row now.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: rival
relations.note: She wants Mid Row 6 for her sister. Her sister has a husband with a roof already; mine have nothing.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: fisher
relations.note: Brings in a good catch and does not argue the count. I like her.

relations.name: Chidi Okoro
relations.label: fisher
relations.note: His line is the best on the island and he charges for it. Fair enough.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: fisher
relations.note: Brings in a catch and loses his drops at counters the same night. I do not like the look of it.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: fisher
relations.note: Young, steady, fishes beside Neve. A good lad, whatever Aldous Quill thinks.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: tally keeper
relations.note: He holds the key to Mid Row 6 in his room. I will have to ask him for it, and he will want it done properly.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She brought Dory into the world and she does not gossip about what she sees.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Runa's boy, and the best hands at the Cone they say. He was born a Tarn's son whatever row he sleeps on, and he does not look down his nose at the Steps.

memories.gist: My husband went out to the Weirs one morning in a flat calm and never came back; they found the boat and not him.
The fever winter took nine, and I stood at the graves on the Crown and counted them, and Runa stood beside me though she had lost Matthias and I had lost no one of my own house.
The storm last autumn took the end rail of the mole and half the slates off Low Row. We spent a week bailing water out of the ground floor.
The first morning I divided the catch alone after my mother's hands gave out, and old Ingrid Morrow watched me do it and said nothing, and that was the whole of her judgement.
Nell was born in the small hours and I held her before Joss did, because I was in the room and he was not.
My mother told me how the lean years came, when the ships stopped and half the town went with them, and how her mother's generation ate roots and kelp and nothing else for a winter.

stances.why: If the count is crooked the whole town goes hungry and I am the one who counted.
Seven of us in one house and a sound empty one standing dry. The Tarns have been on Low Row long enough.
My own sister married a Sarro. I will not have my grandchildren told they are less than anyone.
Dolly Achterberg says the twelve drops are eaten off at her tables. Drops are drops and fish are fish.
It has burned every night of my life. I do not ask who it is for.

sheet.narrative: I am thirty-one, a line fisher like my father was, and I fish the Fish Steps at first light beside Neve Calloway and Ren Sato. My mother divides the catch and I do not argue with her count, not in front of anyone. What I want is a share in the town's glasshouse, number 11, if Tamsin Hollin ever mends it: greens under glass would feed my three children through a bad winter better than any catch. I have asked her and I have asked Oswin Greave, and both of them said they would think on it, which is not a yes. Petra is owed twelve drops by the Marver and I do not like to see her wait for them.
values: doing the count my mother's way
goals: Get a share in glasshouse 11 for the Tarns when it is mended
See Petra paid her twelve drops
Get the family into Mid Row 6 so the children have room
Teach Ansel to hold a line without tangling it
pastimes: a slow game of counters at the Marver with Eamon
mending my own line by the fire of an evening
walking the strand at low water looking for floats
sheet.calling: Fishing is what I know, but what I would love is growing: greens under glass, my own bay, my own row.
sheet.mood: quiet, hopeful, a little anxious

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She runs the house and the catch and I would not cross her, though I have my own mind about the glasshouse.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She works the smokehouse and comes home smelling of it and never complains. She is owed and it eats at me.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: brother
relations.note: My brother. He dreams of the ship and I dream of a glasshouse; we are not so different.

relations.name: Nell Tarn
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is sharp and she knows it. I want her to have better than a fish line if she wants it.

relations.name: Ansel Tarn
relations.label: son
relations.note: He follows Nell everywhere. I will teach him the line when his hands are big enough.

relations.name: Dory Tarn
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: The baby. She has her mother's look about the eyes.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: glazier
relations.note: She decides which glasshouse is mended. I asked her for a share in 11 and she said she would think on it.

relations.name: Oswin Greave
relations.label: head grower
relations.note: He says what is planted where. If I get a share in 11 I will have to work with him.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: fishing partner
relations.note: We fish the same steps every morning. She is good company and a better fisher.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: fishing partner
relations.note: Steady lad. Fishes beside Neve and does not chase the biggest fish, which is a kind of wisdom.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: She owes my wife twelve drops and says it is eaten off at her tables. I do not like it.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: wife's cousin
relations.note: He is Runa's boy and my cousin by marriage, and a good man at the pipe; but he has the Kiln at his back and I am still asking for a share, so I keep it friendly.

relations.name: Runa Sarro
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: My mother's sister, and she has never once made me feel the Tarn in me since she went up to the Sarros. She gives Tamsin the panes, so I ask her how the lehr is doing more often than I need to.

memories.gist: The morning my father did not come back from the Weirs; I was a boy and I went down to the Steps anyway because there was nothing else to do.
The fever winter: I carried water to the sick and did not get it, and Matthias Sarro died two doors from where I stood.
Nell was born, and then Ansel, and then Dory, and each time Mirren Quill put the child in my arms and said 'here is another mouth' and laughed.
The storm last autumn: I held the shutter on the seaward window of Low Row 4 all night while the slates came off the roof above us.
I asked Tamsin Hollin in the Counting House yard about a share in glasshouse 11 and she said she would think on it, and I have thought of nothing else since.

stances.why: Fish and roots are what we have; a share in a glasshouse is what would make a hard winter soft.
I have watched her count since I was a boy and no one has ever shown me a crooked count.
Petra is owed twelve drops and it is not for Dolly Achterberg to decide it is paid in meals.
Whatever I think of the house, I will not shame her at the Steps.
Eamon's ship will take the Hanger's trees and I would rather they went to roof beams and glasshouse frames.

sheet.narrative: I am twenty-seven and I fish the mole at first light, and in the afternoons when the tide lets me I go down to the dry dock and help Bram Calloway with the Second Thought. The hull is framed and she is a beautiful thing, and I mean to have a place on her when she goes. My mother thinks it is a boy's dream; my brother thinks the timber would be better spent on roofs; neither of them has stood in that dock and felt the ribs of a ship that could cross the Combs. I drink at the Marver with Lorcan Vane of an evening and I know what he owes and I say nothing, because it is not mine to say.
goals: Earn a place on the Second Thought when she is finished
Help Bram get the fourteen trees from Marit Sedge
Keep my mother from knowing how much I have given the dry dock
See the far side of the Combs with my own eyes
pastimes: working in the dry dock on free afternoons
drinking at the Marver with Lorcan
walking the mole at dusk to look at the Pale
sheet.calling: The ship. I would give my mornings to the catch forever if I could give my afternoons to the Second Thought and sail her out.
sheet.mood: restless, hopeful, a little reckless

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She thinks the ship is foolishness. She has not seen her.

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He wants a glasshouse and I want a ship. We do not say it to each other but we both know.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: good-sister
relations.note: She is a Vane and she works hard and she is owed. I would speak to Dolly myself if Joss would let me.

relations.name: Nell Tarn
relations.label: niece
relations.note: She wants to come out on the mole with me. When she is a little bigger I will take her.

relations.name: Ansel Tarn
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: A quiet little lad. He will be a fisher or he will be nothing, and both are all right.

relations.name: Dory Tarn
relations.label: niece
relations.note: The baby. She will not remember me being here when she is grown, if I go.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: master
relations.note: He took me on in the dock when no one else would. I would sail with him anywhere.

relations.name: Marit Sedge
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She will not give Bram his trees. I understand her and I do not forgive her.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: drinking friend
relations.note: He owes the Marver and the Counting House and Chidi Okoro and he still buys a round. I like him and I worry for him.

relations.name: Ysolde Calloway
relations.label: master's wife
relations.note: She works the Weirs and does not say much about the ship. I think she is afraid of it.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: fishing partner's daughter
relations.note: Bram's girl. She fishes the Steps and looks at Imre Sarro the way I look at the ship.

relations.name: Imre Sarro
relations.label: fishing neighbour
relations.note: A Kiln man whose mother was a Tarn, so he is half ours and half theirs. He has the best hands at the Cone and he knows it, and Neve Calloway watches him the way I watch the ship.

relations.name: Runa Sarro
relations.label: aunt
relations.note: My mother's sister, who married into the Kilns and never once made us feel small for it. She gives me a warm word at the lehr door and asks after the family before she asks about anything else.

memories.gist: The first afternoon I climbed into the dry dock and Bram handed me a plane and said 'shave that frame', and I did it badly and he made me do it again until it was right.
The night the storm took the mole rail, I was on the mole and I saw the sea come over the stones and I thought: that is what the Combs must be like, and I wanted to see it.
My father went out to the Weirs and did not come back. I was nine and I have fished the mole ever since, because the mole is where he would have come home.
The fever winter took Matthias Sarro, who was a blower and Runa's husband, and I carried peat to the house and did not go in.
Lorcan and I drank at the Marver the night the last of the storm damage came down and he told me he owed nine drops to the Counting House and I bought the next round.

stances.why: I have stood in her ribs. She is sound. If anyone can cross, she can.
Fourteen trees out of seventy, and the Hanger would grow them back. Marit Sedge guards a wood she planted as if it were her child.
Lorcan's drops are Lorcan's business and I will not carry tales to Aldous Quill.
Everyone in Cullet looks at the white and turns away. I look at it and want to know what is behind it.
I fish the mole every morning before I go to the dock. I do not take without giving.

sheet.narrative: I was born a Vane and I married Joss Tarn and now I run smokehouse 1 on the quay, which is the best work I have ever had. Two fish make a measure of oil and four loads of kelp make one of ash, but smoked fish is simpler: salt, smoke, time, and the fish keeps for a month. The Marver has owed me twelve drops since the winter and Dolly Achterberg says it is eaten off at her tables, and I have not decided yet whether to make a fuss of it or let it lie. My brothers Lorcan and Davin are both on Low Row and both a worry to me in different ways, and Sander's boy Wick is at the wash-house most nights with Greta.
goals: Get the twelve drops from Dolly Achterberg or settle it openly
Keep smokehouse 1 the best-kept smokehouse on the quay
See Wick Marl grow up with a mother and uncles who are there for him
Persuade Joss to let her speak to Dolly herself
pastimes: sitting against the wash-house wall in the evening with the other women
walking the quay at dusk to smell the smokehouses
watching Dory sleep
sheet.calling: The smokehouse. I love the work and I am good at it and I would keep it all my life.
sheet.mood: busy, warm, a little tired

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is slow and steady and he worries about the drops for me, which is more than most husbands would.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: good-mother
relations.note: She runs the house and I would not cross her, but she has strong views on the catch and the house.

relations.name: Nell Tarn
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is my eldest and she is clever and she does not know it yet.

relations.name: Ansel Tarn
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is quiet and he follows Nell and he is no trouble at all.

relations.name: Dory Tarn
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My baby. I have her at the smokehouse with me when I can and Greta minds her when I cannot.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He owes everyone in town and he still plays counters every night. I love him and I have told him so.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He works the cart and the wheel and he is good to Wick. He is the steadier of my brothers.

relations.name: Wick Marl
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Sander's boy. He has his father's look and Thessaly is doing well by him.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: She owes me twelve drops and says it is paid in meals. I have not eaten twelve drops at her tables.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She minds Dory and Wick both and she hears everything at the wall and I do not mind her hearing it.

relations.name: Chidi Okoro
relations.label: line-maker
relations.note: Joss buys his line and it is the best on the island and it is dear.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: good-sister
relations.note: She is raising Sander's boy in the dark hours of the night and never once complained to me about it; I give her fish for the smokehouse and she gives me the truth about the Cone.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: good-brother
relations.note: He helps Bram in the dry dock on his free afternoons and drinks with my Lorcan, and I wish he would put his hands to something that pays before the winter.

memories.gist: The fever winter took my brother Sander's wife's sister and half the town, and I carried smoked fish up the wynds to houses with their doors shut.
The first morning I ran smokehouse 1 alone, after the old smoker's hands gave out, and I got the fire right and the first fish came out gold.
Dory was born at dawn and Mirren Quill put her in my arms and said she had her father's chin, which is not true, she has mine.
The storm last autumn took the smokehouse door off its hinges and I sat up all night with the fish and the fire to keep it going.
Dolly Achterberg told me in the Counting House yard that the twelve drops were eaten off at her tables, and I said nothing, and I have been thinking of what to say ever since.
Sander drowned off the mole the winter before Wick was born, and I stood on the quay and watched them drag for him and Thessaly stood beside me and neither of us said a word.

stances.why: Dolly says it is eaten off at her tables. I did not sell her twelve drops of smoked fish for a bowl of her stew.
It is my work and it is the best work I have ever had and I will not have it said it is not kept.
Lorcan owes the town and Wick has no father and I would give my last drop to either of them.
I was born a Vane and married a Tarn and my children will be neither and both and that is fine.
It burns every night and it is a comfort to see it from the smokehouse door, whatever it costs in fish.

sheet.narrative: I am seven and I go to Benedikt Orme's lessons in the mornings and I mind my brother Ansel after, which is not fair because he is four and he cannot keep up. I want to go out on the mole with my uncle Eamon and fish in the dark by the Watchglass light, and he says when I am bigger, and I am nearly bigger. Juno Brandt is my friend and we play at the Fish Steps and I am always the one who divides the catch.
goals: Go out on the mole with Uncle Eamon
Mind Ansel without losing him
Be allowed to hold a real line
pastimes: playing at dividing the catch with Juno Brandt
watching the boats from the Fish Steps
drawing on the slate at lessons
sheet.calling: I want to be a fisher like my grandmother and divide the catch one day.
sheet.mood: bright, impatient, fond

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is quiet and he smells of fish and I love him.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She works the smokehouse and she says I am clever and I am.

relations.name: Ansel Tarn
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He follows me everywhere and I have to mind him and he is no trouble really.

relations.name: Dory Tarn
relations.label: sister
relations.note: The baby. She is little and she is mine to look after when Mother is at the smokehouse.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She divides the catch and everyone does what she says and one day I will.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He fishes the mole and he says he will take me when I am bigger.

relations.name: Juno Brandt
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play at the Steps and she is always the one who is owed drops.

memories.gist: The morning my grandmother let me stand beside her on the Steps while she divided the catch, and I counted the fish out loud and got to twelve before I lost count.
The storm last autumn: the wind came under the door and I hid under the table with Ansel and Mother sang to us.
Dory was born and I was allowed to hold her for the first time and she grabbed my finger.

stances.why: Uncle Eamon says when I am bigger and I am bigger every day.
Mother told me to mind him and I will not let him out of my sight at the Steps.
Grandmother does it every morning and it is the most important thing anyone does.

sheet.narrative: I am four and in the mornings I go down to the Fish Steps with my grandmother and sit on the wall and watch the fishers come in. Nell goes to lessons and I am not allowed to go with her yet. I like the smell of the smokehouse and the sound of the gulls and being carried on Uncle Davin's cart.
goals: Be where Nell is
Be big enough for lessons
Get a ride on Uncle Davin's cart
pastimes: sitting on the wall at the Fish Steps
chasing gulls on the quay
playing with the glass floats outside the door
sheet.calling: I want to fish like my grandmother and my father.
sheet.mood: content, quiet, watchful

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: father
relations.note: He carries me on his shoulders down the wynd.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She smells of smoke and she sings when she puts me to bed.

relations.name: Nell Tarn
relations.label: sister
relations.note: I follow her everywhere and she lets me, mostly.

relations.name: Dory Tarn
relations.label: sister
relations.note: The baby. She cries and I do not like it but she is mine.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She lets me sit on the wall at the Steps and watch.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He lifts me up high and I am not scared at all.

memories.gist: The first time I sat on the wall at the Fish Steps by myself and the fishers came in and I counted them.
The storm came and I hid under the table with Nell and Mother sang.

sheet.narrative: Warm. Milk. My mother's voice and the smoke smell of her. My sister's face close to mine, and someone singing. Then sleep.
pastimes: being held
sleeping
sheet.mood: warm and fed

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: mother
relations.note: Milk and warmth and the smoke smell.

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: father
relations.note: A low voice and big hands that carry me.

relations.name: Nell Tarn
relations.label: sister
relations.note: A face close to mine, always talking.

relations.name: Ansel Tarn
relations.label: brother
relations.note: Another small one who is always near.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: A voice that means food and being held.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: A big loud shape that smells of fish and laughs too near my face.

memories.gist: Being born at dawn and put into my mother's arms.

sheet.narrative: I was born on Low Row and I have fished the Fish Steps since I was nine, but what I am known for is line. I make it from gut and twist and beeswax and patience, and I sell it dear because it is worth dear — every fisher on the island owes their best mornings to my hands. I keep my house and my family and I keep my accounts in my head, and I have decided that my children will read properly, not just write their names like me. The rest of the town can think what it likes about that.
values: a good line is worth its price
a debt is a debt, written or not
the sea gives to those who go early
goals: Get Benedikt Orme to teach Zeke and Ife the formal letters, not just their names
Collect the nine drops Lorcan Vane owes me for line without breaking the house
Build up enough drops to buy a second net loft bench of my own
See Zeke and Ife able to read a tablet before they are grown
pastimes: Twisting and waxing line at the kitchen table of an evening
A slow walk along the quay at dusk, looking at the boats
Sitting at the Marver with a cup, listening to the talk
sheet.calling: Making line — the best on the island — and one day teaching my son the twist of it.
sheet.mood: steady, a little proud, quietly determined

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She is up before me with the tide and back with kelp and sea-glass; I would not trade her for any Kiln wife in the Rows.

relations.name: Zeke Okoro
relations.label: son
relations.note: Quick with his hands and quick to run off to the cullet yard; he will make something of himself if he learns his letters.

relations.name: Ife Okoro
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She follows Zeke everywhere and is sharper than she lets on.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: Owes me nine drops for line and plays counters with the money he should be paying me.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: A good man and the only reader we have; I want more from him than names on a slate.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She divides the catch fair and she has never once shorted me.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: fellow fisher
relations.note: Fishes beside me at the Steps and buys my line; a good hand.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: fellow fisher
relations.note: Young, keen, fishes beside Neve; his father burns the kelp that smokes Low Row.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: cook
relations.note: The Marver is where I take my evenings; she feeds me well enough for the drops.

memories.gist: The fever winter six years ago: I carried fish to the shut houses and stayed well, and I still do not know why I was spared.
The first time I twisted a line that Neve Calloway said was better than her father's — she bought three lengths and paid in drops.
The storm last autumn took the end rail of the mole and half the slates off Low Row; we spent a week drying out.
The morning Zeke was born, before dawn, and I had already been to the Steps and back.
Lorcan Vane took four lengths of line on trust and has not paid; I have not written it in the ledger, because we are neighbours.

stances.why: I make the best line on the island and I will not sell it cheap.
I can write my name and no more, and I will not have my children held back the same way.
A man who does not pay what he owes is a man you cannot trust with anything.
The Cone needs ash and the plots need kelp, and Nan Fenwick is not the only one who needs it.
Everything worth hearing is heard at the Marver of an evening.

sheet.narrative: I go down to the Wrack Strand with the tide, whatever hour it is, and I gather kelp for the plots and the ash house. But what I love is the sea-glass — green and amber and one rare blue — and I know which wreck each colour came from, because my mother told me and her mother told her. I carry kelp up the wynds to Nan Fenwick's plots and it is never as much as she wants. I keep my house and my children and my glass, and I am content enough.
values: the sea gives and the sea takes
every colour of glass has a story
a neighbour is owed what you can carry
my children before my own ease
keep what the sea throws up
goals: Learn which wreck the rarest blue sea-glass came from
Keep Zeke and Ife fed and at their lessons
Carry enough kelp up the wynds to keep Nan Fenwick off my back
One day lay out my sea-glass on a board by colour, like Ode's sill of cullet
pastimes: Sorting sea-glass by colour on the kitchen table
Walking the Wrack Strand at low tide, alone
Sitting against the warm wall of the wash-house of an evening
sheet.calling: Reading the sea-glass — knowing which wreck each colour came from, and passing it on.
sheet.mood: calm, watchful, a little tired

relations.name: Chidi Okoro
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He makes the best line on the island and he is a good man, though he worries too much about letters.

relations.name: Zeke Okoro
relations.label: son
relations.note: He wants to find me a colour I have never seen; I hope he does.

relations.name: Ife Okoro
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is the one who will remember the wrecks after me.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: fellow gatherer
relations.note: We gather side by side and she agrees with me that the smoke lies too low on Low Row.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: fellow gatherer
relations.note: A strange girl, full of ships and sails, but a good worker on the strand.

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: root grower
relations.note: She wants more kelp than three women can carry up the wynds, and she says so every time.

relations.name: Kenji Sato
relations.label: ash burner
relations.note: His kilns take the kelp the plots want; his smoke lies on my washing.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: porter
relations.note: He carts the kelp up the wynds when Nan pays him, and he is fair about it.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: wash-house keeper
relations.note: She hears everything at the warm wall and tells me most of it.

memories.gist: My mother showing me a blue piece of sea-glass and telling me it came from a ship that broke on the Combs before I was born.
The fever winter: I kept the house and fed whoever came to the door, and I did not lose a child.
The storm last autumn: the kelp came up in heaps after it, more than I had ever seen, and we gathered for days.
The morning Ife was born and Zeke would not leave the door.
Nan Fenwick telling me on the wynd that I had brought half what the plots needed, and me saying nothing.

stances.why: My mother knew it and her mother before her, and I will not let it be forgotten.
I have seen it give kelp in heaps and take men off the mole.
We all live off the same strand and the same plots.
It spoils the washing and the air, and the kilns could be set further upwind.
They are the whole of what I have.

sheet.narrative: I am eleven and I go to Benedikt's lessons in the mornings, but what I like best is the cullet yard with Edda Hollin and the others, hunting the coloured glass. My mother knows every wreck the sea-glass came from, and I mean to find her a colour she has never seen. I am quick and I am not afraid of the shed, though Ode Pontil chases us out of it.
values: a new colour is worth a scolding
my mother knows everything about glass
goals: Find a colour of sea-glass my mother has never seen
Keep up with Edda Hollin and the bigger children in the cullet yard
pastimes: Hunting coloured cullet in the cullet yard
Playing at the Fish Steps with the other children
sheet.calling: Finding glass — the rarer the colour the better.
sheet.mood: restless, eager

relations.name: Chidi Okoro
relations.label: father
relations.note: He wants me to learn letters and I would rather be in the yard.

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She knows every wreck the sea-glass came from and I want to bring her a new one.

relations.name: Ife Okoro
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She follows me everywhere and is better at the lessons than me.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: leader
relations.note: She leads us into the cullet yard and knows where the best colours are.

relations.name: Lumi Pontil
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She goes to the Cone before dawn and knows things about glass I do not.

relations.name: Ode Pontil
relations.label: the man who chases us
relations.note: He shouts at us to get out of the heaps, but he keeps the best colours on his sill.

memories.gist: Finding a piece of amber cullet in the yard and Edda Hollin saying it was the best anyone had found that week.
My mother showing me the blue sea-glass and saying there was no other like it on the island.
Ode Pontil catching me in the cullet heaps and chasing me out with a shout.

stances.why: The best pieces are always where you are not supposed to go.
She is the oldest and she found the way in.

sheet.narrative: I am nine and I go to Benedikt's lessons with Zeke, and in the afternoons I play in the cullet yard with Lumi Pontil, who is my best friend. Lumi goes to the Cone before dawn with her grandmother and tells me about the colours of the melt, and I tell her about the sea-glass my mother finds. I want to keep up with Zeke, and mostly I do.
values: the sea-glass belongs to my mother
goals: Keep up with Zeke in the yard and at the lessons
See the Cone's fire up close one day with Lumi
pastimes: Playing in the cullet yard with Lumi Pontil
Sorting sea-glass with my mother
sheet.calling: Not yet — but I like the glass and the colours.
sheet.mood: bright, a little shy

relations.name: Chidi Okoro
relations.label: father
relations.note: He says I am sharper than I let on.

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She lets me sort the sea-glass with her and tells me the wrecks.

relations.name: Zeke Okoro
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He runs ahead of me everywhere and I am always trying to catch up.

relations.name: Lumi Pontil
relations.label: best friend
relations.note: She tells me about the Cone and I tell her about the sea-glass, and we trade.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: leader
relations.note: She leads the yard and lets me come along.

memories.gist: Lumi Pontil telling me the names of the colours of the melt, and me not being able to remember them all.
My mother letting me hold the blue sea-glass for the first time.
The first day at Benedikt's lessons, when I could write my own name before Zeke could.

stances.why: She has been going there before dawn since she was small.
He is my brother and I will not be left behind.

sheet.narrative: I'm a Vane of Low Row, and I fish the Fish Steps at first light like my father did before the fever took him. The mornings are honest; it's the nights that cost me. Under the arcade, with the counters warm in my hand, I can feel a run coming — and then Roos or old Aldous takes it off me and I owe a little more. I mean to win it all back one night. Davin doesn't say much about it, which is worse than if he shouted.
goals: Win back everything I owe in one good night at counters
Pay off the nine drops written in Aldous Quill's ledger
Settle with Dolly at the Marver before she stops serving me
See Wick grow up knowing his father's brothers
pastimes: Counters under the arcade every night
Sitting on the quay edge mending a line at dusk
A mug at the Marver with Eamon Tarn
sheet.calling: Line fishing at first light is the work I was made for; I'd be content if the nights didn't undo it.
sheet.mood: hopeful and a little frayed

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: brother
relations.note: Steady as a stone, and he never once scolds me for the counters. I'd do the same for him.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She runs the smokehouse and a house of five and still asks after me. She got the better of the three of us.

relations.name: Wick Marl
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Sander's boy. I owe it to Sander to be something Wick can look at.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: Wick's mother
relations.note: Night watch at the Cone, and she never asks me for a drop. I respect that more than I say.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: tally keeper
relations.note: He writes my losses neat as a grave marker and never loses himself. Nine drops, in his book, in his hand.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: counters rival
relations.note: She takes my drops most nights and smiles doing it. One night the board will turn.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: Good cook, sharp eye. She's kept my tab open longer than she should have.

relations.name: Chidi Okoro
relations.label: line-maker
relations.note: Best line on the island and he knows it. I owe him for the last spool and he hasn't pressed me.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: drinking friend
relations.note: My sister's good-brother. We put the town to rights at the Marver most evenings.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: fellow fisher
relations.note: Fishes beside me at the Steps and outs me every time. Sharp tongue, good hand.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: catch divider
relations.note: She divides fair, even to a Vane who owes everybody. I'd not cross her.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: night fisher
relations.note: Fishes the mole by the lamp while I'm losing at counters. Sensible man.

memories.gist: The fever winter: Sander went out to the mole in the cold and never came back, and Wick was born the next winter without him.
The night I won four drops straight off Roos and felt like the best player in Cullet — then gave them all back before the arcade emptied.
Aldous Quill reading my name out of the ledger in front of the arches, and the nine drops going in the book in his neat hand.
Last autumn's storm took the end rail of the mole; I helped Davin and the others haul the broken timber up before the sea got it.
A morning at the Fish Steps when the fish came so thick Magda gave me a double share, and I carried half of it to Petra's smokehouse.
Davin pushing the handcart up the wynd with a load of peat, and me thinking he works harder than any of us and gets no notice for it.

stances.why: Every loss is just the board waiting to turn; I've felt the run coming.
Sander's gone and Wick's here; whatever I owe, the Vanes stand together.
The book is open to anyone who asks, and my name's in it in Aldous's hand.
Whatever the night takes, the morning catch is clean and mine.
He's never once mentioned my debts and I'd rather not hear him start.

sheet.narrative: I push the handcart and walk the Heron's wheel, and the town pays me a drop here and there for it. It's not a trade, whatever anyone says — a man wants something he can hand down. Lorcan's my brother and he's drowning in drops a little at a time, so I've been paying a bit of it off quiet, through Dolly, with Aldous writing it. He mustn't know. He'd take it as pity, and it isn't that.
values: a trade to call my own
goals: Find work that is mine, not just carrying for others
Clear the rest of Lorcan's Marver debt without him finding out
Save enough drops to set up properly one day
Keep Wick and Petra from ever needing to worry about the brothers
pastimes: Walking the strand at low tide looking at what the sea's left
A quiet mug at the Marver after the cart's put away
Riding Wick on the handcart when the load's light
sheet.calling: I'd be a boatwright or a smith if the island had room for another — something where the work stays made after the day's done.
sheet.mood: quiet and a little worn

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He'd give me his last drop if I asked, which is exactly why he's in the book and I'm not.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She's got a head for the smokehouse and a heart for all of us. I'd tell her anything but this.

relations.name: Wick Marl
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Sander's boy. When I put him on the cart he laughs the whole length of Low Row.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: keeper of my secret
relations.note: She took the six drops without a word and put it against Lorcan's tab. She's never breathed it.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: tally keeper
relations.note: He wrote it in the book as I asked and said nothing more. A careful man.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: Wick's mother
relations.note: She works the night watch and trusts me with her boy's name. I'd not let her down.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: the boatwright
relations.note: I walk his wheel when he lifts a load. He builds a ship and I carry for it; I'd like to build something.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: peat man
relations.note: I cart his peat down and he pays fair. He grumbles about the Cone's price and I listen.

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: customer
relations.note: She pays me to cart kelp up the wynds and always wants more than the gatherers bring.

relations.name: Eamon Tarn
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He drinks with Lorcan at the Marver. I keep my mouth shut and drink with them.

relations.name: Kit Calloway
relations.label: young friend
relations.note: A boy who wants to be something. I know how that feels and I've told him so.

memories.gist: The fever winter: Sander drowned off the mole in the cold, and I carried his body up with Lorcan and could not speak.
Dolly counting six drops into her palm at the Marver's back door and saying she'd put it on Lorcan's tab and tell no one.
Aldous Quill writing the six drops in the ledger in his neat hand and asking me once, only once, if I was sure.
Walking the Heron's wheel all afternoon while Bram lifted the new frame timber into the dry dock, and my legs shaking after.
The storm last autumn took slates off Low Row and I spent two days hauling them down to Gwil Stannard's cart.
Putting Wick on the empty handcart and running him along the quay, and him shouting for more.

stances.why: If Lorcan knew, he'd never take another drop from me, and he'd sink.
Anyone with a back can push a cart; I want work that leaves something standing.
The whole town talks at the wash-house wall and I'd rather not be talked about.
Aldous keeps it straight; better a written debt than a remembered one.
Kit and Wick will need someone to tell them the truth and not laugh at them.

sheet.secret: I have paid six drops of Lorcan's debt to the Marver without telling him. Dolly knows, and Aldous wrote it.

sheet.narrative: I have mended nets on the Fish Steps for forty years, and I move my bench with the sun because a net-mender who sits in her own shadow works blind. I raised Lark from a baby when the fever took my Siri, and I have done it alone, and I will not have her head turned by a light on a rock and a story about a sail. The sea gives what it gives and takes what it takes; a woman who waits for ships waits hungry. I keep my bench, my needles and my granddaughter, and I mean to keep all three.
values: the sea is not a story
keep to what you can see
goals: Get Lark to let the sail go and settle to the wrack and the town
Keep the two of us fed and the roof patched through another winter
Mend well for Magda's house so the work keeps coming
Live to see Lark married or settled, to someone of the island
pastimes: Mending nets at her bench in the sun
Sitting against the wash-house wall in the evening, listening
Walking the Fish Steps at low water to see what the tide left
sheet.calling: The nets: a well-mended net is the difference between a full boat and a hungry house, and I am the best there is at it.
sheet.mood: Wearied, watchful, quietly stubborn

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: granddaughter
relations.note: The last of my Siri, and the whole of my worry. I love her and I cannot make her see sense.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: old friend
relations.note: I mend her house's nets and she divides my share of the catch fairly. We have buried the same people.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: the lamp keeper
relations.note: A decent man with a fool's vow. His light fills my girl's head with ships.

relations.name: Livia Faro
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good girl, but she and Lark talk at the mole at dusk and I know what they talk about.

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She keeps an eye on Lark on the strand, and I am glad of it.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We are of an age and have both buried too much. She complains about the smoke and I let her.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A widower like me, and he fishes the night alone. I send him a fish when I have one to spare.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her smokehouse keeps my fish through the week. Her brother Sander's boy is her cross and she carries it.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: wash-house
relations.note: She hears everything and tells half of it. I sit at her wall and say nothing worth hearing.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: the reader
relations.note: He fills children's heads with the old script. I never learned it and I have not starved for it.

memories.gist: The fever winter: my Siri died in the bed above me and I could not get the healer there in time. I have never forgiven the cold of that room.
Lark at three, sitting on my bench tangling my best line and laughing. That was before Siri went.
My mother told me how her own mother remembered the lean years, when half the town's roofs came off for fuel and there was no wood left to mend them.
Last spring Lark came running up the Fish Steps saying she had seen a sail, and I looked where she pointed and saw white water and grey and the Pale, and nothing else.
Mending Magda's big net the morning after the autumn storm, with the slates down all round the town and the mole's end rail gone.
Anselm Faro lighting the Watchglass at dusk, and Lark not ten steps from him, watching, as she does every night.

stances.why: Oil that could be eaten burns every night for a ship that will never come. I have said so at the wall and been told to hush.
I looked where she pointed. There was nothing but the Combs and the Pale. A girl at dusk sees what she wants.
When Siri died I went back to the bench the next day, and it kept me.
Greta Dunmore hears everything said at her wall. I have learned to say little there.
The Kiln families have never taken a Strand apprentice at the Cone, and the old line does not wash out.

sheet.narrative: I saw it. I was on the mole at dusk in the last of the light and there was a sail beyond the Combs, white and leaning, for as long as it takes to say so, and then the Pale had it. Nobody believes me, not my grandmother, not Amara, not Ingrid's friends at the wall. I gather kelp in the cold mornings and I watch the water every dusk, and I will see it again. The lamp is lit for it. That is what the vow means, whatever the old people say.
values: I will not be talked out of it
goals: See the sail again, and prove it was real
Find someone who believes her, or a way to make them
Keep gathering enough kelp to hold her place and her grandmother's temper
Get out beyond the harbour mouth somehow, one day
pastimes: Standing at the tip of the mole at dusk to watch the lamp lit
Walking the Wrack Strand looking for sea-glass and wreck colour
Talking with Livia Faro at the lamp house
sheet.calling: The water beyond the Combs. I want to be the one who goes and looks, not the one who mends nets and waits.
sheet.mood: Restless, hurt, lit up

relations.name: Ingrid Morrow
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She raised me and she thinks I am a fool. I love her and I cannot make her look.

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She gathers beside me and does not laugh at me, though she does not believe me either.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Kind, and tired, and says the smoke gets in everything. She listens better than most.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: the lamp keeper
relations.note: He lights it every night and never mocks me for watching. He keeps the vow I believe in.

relations.name: Livia Faro
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We talk at the mole at dusk. She does not say I am wrong, and that is worth a great deal.

relations.name: Col Roon
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: He walks the strand when I do and has never spoken to me. I think he is shy. I think I might speak first.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: elder
relations.note: She divides the catch and my grandmother mends her nets. She looks at me as if I were a broken thing.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: the boatwright
relations.note: He is building a ship in the dry dock. If anyone could cross the Combs it is him, and he needs trees he cannot have.

memories.gist: The dusk last spring on the mole: a sail beyond the Combs, white and leaning, for as long as it takes to say so, then the Pale closed over it.
My mother Siri dying in the fever winter, and Ingrid's hands on my shoulders in the graveyard on the Crown, and the glass marker they chose for her.
Telling the whole Fish Steps what I saw, and the silence, and Lorcan Vane laughing, and Ingrid telling me to hush.
Gathering kelp with Amara and Hana in a cold wind, and Amara showing me which wreck a piece of blue sea-glass came from, as if the sea had a memory.
Standing at the tip of the mole while Anselm Faro lit the Watchglass, and the blue band in it, and thinking: that is for the sail.

stances.why: It was not a wave or a bird. It was a sail, and I will not say otherwise to be comfortable.
The first keeper swore the light would burn until the ships came back. Why swear it if it means nothing?
Ingrid and her friends talk only of what the sea takes. Nobody talks of what it might bring.
The ships crossed them once. Nothing has changed about the water except that we stopped trying.
I gather my kelp before I go to the mole. Ingrid would turn me out otherwise, and I would deserve it.

sheet.narrative: I burn kelp on the strand for the Cone's ash, and I have done it since I was a lad of fifteen. The smoke goes where the wind takes it, and the wind takes it over Low Row, and Greta Dunmore tells me about it every burning day as if I could turn the wind with a word. My wife tells me too, softer, and that is worse. I sell my ash to Vessa Pontil and she pays me in drops, and the Cone runs on what I burn, whatever anyone says about their washing.
goals: Burn my kelp without being told about the smoke every time
Get a fair price from Vessa Pontil for the ash
See Ren settled with a good wife, though the Quill girl worries me
pastimes: Mending my kiln rakes by the ash house
A quiet mug at the Marver with Tam Roon
Watching the gulls work the strand at low tide
sheet.calling: I love a clean burn — kelp going to ash just right, neither underdone nor clinkered. That is my craft.
sheet.mood: Gruff and put-upon, but steady

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She wants a house away from my smoke. I hear it every burning day, and I love her for saying it plain.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: son
relations.note: Good fisher, better than I ever was at the line. I hope the Quill girl sees it.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Tells me about the smoke as if I chose the wind. I have heard it a hundred times.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: She buys my ash and pays fair enough, but she could pay better for what the Cone lives on.

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: fellow worker
relations.note: Gathers beside my wife. Good hands, and she does not lecture me.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: fellow worker
relations.note: A strange girl with her sail, but she works the wrack hard.

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: rival for kelp
relations.note: She wants the kelp for her plots that I want for the kilns. We are both right.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Drinks at the Marver and does not tell me how to burn.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: the girl's father
relations.note: He looks at my son as if he were a bad debt. I keep my peace about it.

memories.gist: The fever winter: Hana and I kept the kilns going while half the town was sick, and we buried neighbours we had known all our lives.
The first day I burned kelp alone, my father watching from the ash house door, and the ash came out grey and good.
Greta Dunmore came down to the strand in person last summer to tell me the smoke was on her washing, and I said the wind was not mine to command.
Ren brought home his first line-caught fish and I smoked it myself on a bit of driftwood fire.
Last autumn's storm tore the kiln shelter apart and I rebuilt it with driftwood and old slate in three days.

stances.why: The Cone needs ash and the ash comes from kelp. No ash, no glass, no town.
I cannot command the wind, and I am tired of being treated as if I could.
My wife and son come before anyone's washing.
Aldous Quill's face when my son speaks to his daughter says it plainly enough.

sheet.narrative: I gather wrack on the Wrack Strand with Amara and Lark, and on burning days I come home to a house that smells of my husband's kilns. I have asked Kenji for a house further up the row, and he hears me, but nothing moves. Ren is courting the tally keeper's daughter and I am proud of him and afraid for him at once, because the Quills are not our kind and Aldous Quill has a way of looking at a Sato. I keep my peace and gather my kelp and say a word to Greta at the wash-house wall when the smoke is bad.
goals: Move to a house away from the kiln smoke
See Ren happy, whether with Sabine Quill or another
Keep my gathering share against Nan Fenwick's demands
pastimes: Sitting at the wash-house wall with Greta in the evenings
Sorting sea-glass on the strand
Singing the old strand songs while I gather
sheet.calling: I love the strand at first light, the kelp wet and the gulls crying, before the smoke starts.
sheet.mood: Tired and worried, but warm

relations.name: Kenji Sato
relations.label: husband
relations.note: I love him, and I wish he would hear me about the smoke.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy, courting above himself and not seeing it.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She hears everything at the wall and understands about the smoke.

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: fellow gatherer
relations.note: Good company on the strand, and she does not hurry me.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: fellow gatherer
relations.note: A dreamer, but a hard worker, and kind.

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: root grower
relations.note: She wants more kelp than we can carry and does not see the kilns want it too.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: my son's sweetheart
relations.note: A clever girl. I am not sure she knows what she wants, and that frightens me for Ren.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: the tally keeper
relations.note: He does not approve of my son, and he does not hide it.

memories.gist: The fever winter: I nursed Ren through it and lost neighbours I had gathered beside for years, and the smoke of the kilns was the only thing that did not stop.
The day Ren first spoke of Sabine Quill, his face lit up, and I felt both glad and afraid.
A burning day last summer when the smoke lay so thick on Low Row that I washed the linen twice and it still smelled of kelp.
Gathering with my mother as a girl, learning which kelp makes the best ash and which the plots want.
The storm of last autumn took the roof off the ash house shelter, and Kenji and I held the kiln fire through the night.

stances.why: I have lived in it for twenty years and I want one clean room before I am old.
It is in the way Aldous Quill speaks to Ren, and I will not have my son made small.
The plots and the kilns both want it, and neither should starve the other.
Greta hears everything and I would rather she heard me kindly.

sheet.narrative: I fish the Fish Steps at first light beside Neve Calloway and bring my catch to Magda Tarn, and in the evenings I go up to the Crown bench or down to the Fish Steps again. I am courting Sabine Quill, and her father looks at me as if I were a debt he did not agree to, and Sabine herself is not sure, which is worse than her father. I know what my mother fears and I go on anyway, because when Sabine reads the tablets aloud her voice changes and I want to be near that.
goals: Win Sabine Quill, and her father's grudging consent
Make a name as a fisher worth the line Chidi Okoro sells
See my parents in a better house
pastimes: Sitting on the Crown bench at dusk with the whole town below
Playing counters under the arcade, badly
Walking the mole to watch the Watchglass lit
sheet.calling: I love the line and the first light on the water, and I would love it more if I could read the tablets beside Sabine.
sheet.mood: Hopeful and anxious in equal measure

relations.name: Kenji Sato
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me the kilns and the sea both, and he does not say much about Sabine.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She worries about the Quills and me, and I love her for it and wish she would not.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: sweetheart
relations.note: She reads the old script like music. I would wait a long time for her.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: her father
relations.note: He does not approve and does not hide it. I mean to prove him wrong.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: her mother
relations.note: She is kinder than her husband, and I think she sees more.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: fellow fisher
relations.note: We fish the Steps together and she never asks me about Sabine unless I start it.

relations.name: Chidi Okoro
relations.label: line-maker
relations.note: His line is the best on the island and he knows it. I pay what he asks.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: the catch
relations.note: She divides the catch fair and does not play favourites.

relations.name: Joss Tarn
relations.label: fellow fisher
relations.note: We fish the Steps side by side most mornings and he never once needled me about the Quills, though he has asked after glasshouse 11 enough that I know what he is after.

memories.gist: The first time Sabine read a tablet to me in the Readers' House, and I understood not one word but loved the sound.
My first morning on the Fish Steps with my father, and the catch I brought to Magda Tarn with my hands shaking.
The fever winter, when I was fourteen and sick myself, and my mother nursed me while neighbours died.
Aldous Quill looked at me across the Counting House yard and said nothing, and that was worse than anything he could have said.
A night under the arcade when I won three drops from Lorcan Vane and felt, for an hour, like a man of the town.

stances.why: Sabine is worth her father's frown and my mother's worry.
I bring food to the town's tables and I will not be made small for it.
Aldous Quill will not be moved by anger, and Sabine will not be hurried.
Sabine loves it, and I would understand what she loves.

sheet.narrative: I fish the mole by the Watchglass's light, ten till three, when the fish come to it. I've done it since Maddy died, because the nights are mine and the days are Tilly's, and I can be there when she wakes. I keep the lamp company and Anselm keeps mine; he's the only man I talk to most nights. Tilly is all I've got, and I want her to have more than a damp house on Low Row and a father who smells of fish.
goals: See Tilly learn her letters and numbers well enough to choose her own life.
Keep the night fishing good enough to pay the Store and put a little by.
Make the house warmer and drier before next winter.
pastimes: Sitting on the mole at the end of the night, watching the sky pale
Mending his own lines by the hearth
Playing counters at the Marver when he wakes early enough
sheet.calling: Night fishing by the lamp: the one work that fits a man who must be awake when his daughter sleeps.
sheet.mood: Quietly tired, steady, a little lonely.

relations.name: Tilly Dunlin
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: The whole of it. I'd stand on the mole till dawn every night for her.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We keep each other's nights. He talks about ships; I listen.

relations.name: Thessaly Marl
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She takes her break on the mole and we talk. She's got a hard row and doesn't complain.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: smoker
relations.note: She smokes what I catch and pays fair. Her brother Sander was a good man.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: catch-divider
relations.note: She divides the catch and doesn't cheat a night fisher.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: cook
relations.note: The Marver is where I eat when I wake. She lets me sit quiet.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She minds Tilly some evenings. Hears everything, says little to me.

relations.name: Livia Faro
relations.label: lamp-oil
relations.note: Anselm's niece. She buys fish for oil and never haggles too hard.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Building his ship. I don't see the sense, but he's a decent man.

memories.gist: The fever winter: Maddy burning up in our bed, Mirren Quill coming and going, and then the glass slab on the Crown.
The first night I fished by the Watchglass after Maddy died, Anselm didn't say a word, just left the lamp burning and sat with me a while.
A night last autumn when the fish came so thick I filled the boat twice and had to give half away before it spoiled.
Tilly's first day at Benedikt's lessons; she came home spelling her own name and wouldn't stop.
The storm last autumn took the end rail of the mole; I was out there that night and thought the light would go.
My father telling me the lean years' stories: how the roofs came off the empty houses for fuel, and how his mother cried when the last ship didn't come back.

stances.why: It's the only light on the water, and Anselm's vow is the town's. I fish by it and I'd not see it go out.
Magda divides my catch like any other. I earn my bread.
Maddy's gone. Tilly is what I have left to do right.
I've seen men go to cullet over counters. I pay as I go.
Night fishing taught me that. Patience and the lamp, and the fish come.

sheet.narrative: I live with my father on Low Row. He fishes at night and sleeps in the morning, so I'm quiet then. I go to Benedikt's lessons and I like the tablets, and I like Posy. At night I want to stay up with Father and watch the light, but mostly I go to bed. I miss my mother, though I don't say so much.
goals: Stay up late with Father by the Watchglass.
Learn to read the hard tablet in Benedikt's room.
Have Posy come and sleep over at Low Row 1.
pastimes: Playing counters with cullet pieces
Watching the light come on at dusk
Drawing the Watchglass in the sand
sheet.calling: I want to be a reader, or maybe keep the light like Anselm.
sheet.mood: Curious, a little wistful, mostly cheerful.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: father
relations.note: He's tired a lot, but he always has time for me before he goes out.

relations.name: Posy Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We sit together at lessons and play in the cullet yard.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: He's patient and he knows everything about the old writing.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: lamp keeper
relations.note: He lets me watch him light the lamp. He smells of oil.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: minder
relations.note: She minds me sometimes and gives me bread.

memories.gist: The night Father first took me out to the mole to see the light; I was small and he carried me.
My mother's glass slab on the Crown, pale green; Father says she chose it herself.
The day Benedikt showed us the tablet with the island drawn on it, and I found our house on it.

stances.why: He's the one who's always there.
Anselm says it burns every night. I like that it does.
I want to read the hard tablets like Sabine.

sheet.narrative: I have said what grows where on the Ladder for nineteen years, and I say it still: every pane under glass should be feeding someone. My own glasshouse, number six, has been open to the weather since the storm took its roof, and I look at it every morning on my way to number one and feel it like a hole in my pocket. Cora Stannard has flowers in a corner of glasshouse four, and pretty as they are, flowers are not roots. I am fifty-seven, I have a son who grows a tree that does not fruit, and I have less patience than I had at forty, which everyone may make of what they like.
values: the Ladder is one garden and someone must say what goes where
work done at the hour it is set
family, even when it tries me
goals: Get glasshouse 6 glazed and growing again, before any other broken house
Get the corner of glasshouse 4 back into greens
Have the bay in glasshouse 9 turned back to food
See a grandchild born and the house still standing round it
pastimes: Walking the Ladder at dusk when the panes light up, counting which houses are working
A cup at the Marver terrace with Halvard Dunmore, arguing about the old days
Keeping a row of seed heads on the sill and sorting them by hand
sheet.calling: Head grower: I want every pane on the Ladder green with food, and I would rather be the man who says so than the man who is liked.
sheet.mood: Stubborn and a little worn, with the storm's damage still in front of him every day.

relations.name: Elke Greave
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She works two houses down from me and we say the same things about the Ladder without needing to talk.

relations.name: Jory Greave
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good grower with one foolishness in him, and that bay of his eats at me.

relations.name: Suri Greave
relations.label: daughter-in-law
relations.note: Steady hands and a Frit's eye; she will do well here if the boy gives her a house.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: glazier
relations.note: She holds the panes and so holds my glasshouse in her hands. I have asked her plainly for six first.

relations.name: Cora Stannard
relations.label: grower
relations.note: Her flowers are handsome and they are not food, and that corner is food's by right.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She hears everything at that wall and tells it back with interest.

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: fellow grower
relations.note: Roots and greens go to the same table; we trade seed and complaints.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: Her Cone cracks the panes and her Pontil glasshouse is one of the broken ones; she will look to her own first, as I would.

relations.name: Marit Sedge
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She gave my boy his seed, which I have not forgotten, though I wish she had not.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: cook
relations.note: Her terrace is where a man can sit of an evening and hear the town.

memories.gist: The morning after the storm I walked the Ladder and counted three houses open to the sky, and one of them was mine.
The day I was made head grower, old Fenwick's mother put the planting list in my hand and told me it was mine to keep straight.
Jory brought the seed home from Marit Sedge's cottage in his fist and I told him a bay is not a garden bed.
The fever winter: we lost no one in this house, and I have never quite stopped feeling that we were let off.
Cora Stannard put flowers in the corner of glasshouse four and I said nothing for a season, and now it has been three years.
My father told me the lean years' story: how the wood was cut to stumps and the plots were what stood between the town and nothing.

stances.why: The plots and the Ladder are what stands between this town and hunger, and I have seen the lean years' stories come true in a bad winter.
If everyone plants what they like the Ladder is a garden and not a larder.
Glasshouse six feeds a household; the town's eleven can wait a little and the Pontils have their own means.
I was told plainly and it did me no harm.
A fire that is not fed goes out, and the Roons cut what keeps the Ladder warm.

sheet.narrative: I have grown greens under glass for thirty years and I still like the smell of a warm house in the morning. Oswin is a good man and a hard one, and I have learned to let him be hard at the Ladder and softer at the table. My boy has a tree in a bay that has not fruited in three years, and I have bitten my tongue about it until it aches. Suri is carrying, and I find I am counting the weeks more than I count the rows.
values: a warm house and a full table
keeping the peace where it can be kept
goals: See Suri brought to bed safely and the baby strong
Have Jory give up the tree's bay without a quarrel that splits the house
Keep Oswin from making an enemy of Cora Stannard over a corner of flowers
A little more glass and a little less wind in the houses before next winter
pastimes: Sitting at the wash-house wall of an evening with Greta Dunmore
Drying seed heads and swapping them with Nan Fenwick
Singing the old planting songs while she works, badly
sheet.calling: A grower, and glad of it; my calling is a full table and a quiet house, and the Ladder is how I pay for both.
sheet.mood: Anxious and warm, with her worry turned toward the baby and her son.

relations.name: Oswin Greave
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Hard at the Ladder and soft at home, and I would not swap him, though I have thought about it.

relations.name: Jory Greave
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy, wasting a bay on a tree, and I cannot say it to his face without it sounding like his father.

relations.name: Suri Greave
relations.label: daughter-in-law
relations.note: Fond of her as my own; she is carrying and I watch her lift things she should not.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: friend
relations.note: The wash-house wall is where the town is really governed, and Greta keeps the minutes.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: glazier
relations.note: Suri's sister, and the one who decides which of us gets glass; I am civil to her and mean it.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She will have Suri's baby and she has laid out half the Crown; I trust her hands.

relations.name: Cora Stannard
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her flowers are the prettiest thing on the Ladder and Oswin has no eye for it.

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: fellow grower
relations.note: We trade seed and complaints and neither of us is ever satisfied.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: cook
relations.note: A meal at the Marver is a treat and Oswin counts the drops.

memories.gist: The night the storm came I lay listening to slates go and thought of the glass, and in the morning three houses were open.
The fever winter: I nursed nobody and buried nobody and I have never felt clean about it.
Jory's wedding to Suri, in the Counting House yard, with the whole Ladder there and Oswin almost smiling.
The day Suri told me she was expecting, at the wash-house wall, and I sat down on the bench.
My mother's story of the lean years: roofs stripped for fuel and her mother counting roots in the dark.
The first morning Jory's tree was in its bay and he stood there with the seed packet empty in his hand.

stances.why: A house can be argued about any day; a child comes once.
I have seen families split over less than a bay of glass, and I will not have mine.
If I do not hear what is said at the wall I cannot look after my own.
I had mine and my mother let it be, and here I am.
I love Cora's flowers, but a flower does not feed a child, and I know which I would choose.

sheet.narrative: I am twenty-five and I have grown a tree for three years in a bay of glasshouse nine, and it has not fruited, and I still believe it will. My father thinks the bay should be greens and says so at the table, and my mother says nothing and says it louder. Suri and I live in my parents' house, which is not the fault of any of us, and I would give her a door of her own tomorrow if I could. I grafted the thing myself from a slip Marit Sedge gave me, and I have kept it alive through two bad winters, and I am not going to turn it into cabbages because it has been slow.
values: a man should finish what he starts
Suri before the rest of it
the old knowledge of grafting and seed
not being told what to plant in my own bay
goals: Get one fruit off the tree, and then another
A house of their own before the baby comes, or soon after
Learn from Marit Sedge how the tree was grown before the Hanger
Keep the bay without a war in the house
pastimes: Sitting in glasshouse 9 at dusk with the tree, pinching off shoots
Walking up to the Hanger to gather fallen branches and talk to Marit Sedge
Playing counters under the arcade on the nights he can spare the drops
sheet.calling: To grow something that was not here before, and to hand it on; the tree is the beginning of that and the rest is patience.
sheet.mood: Quietly stubborn, a little bruised by his father's judgement, and hopeful in a way he does not say aloud.

relations.name: Suri Greave
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She is the one person I do not have to explain the tree to, and she is carrying our child.

relations.name: Oswin Greave
relations.label: father
relations.note: He says the bay should grow greens and I hear it every meal; he is not wrong and he is not right.

relations.name: Elke Greave
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She says nothing and I know what the nothing means, and it stings more than my father.

relations.name: Marit Sedge
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: She gave me the slip and did not laugh at me, and she has more patience with trees than anyone in town.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: sister-in-law
relations.note: Suri's sister, and the one who could put glass over my bay if she chose.

relations.name: Cora Stannard
relations.label: fellow grower
relations.note: She grows flowers and takes the same grief from my father, and we have that between us.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Everything I say at the wall will be known by evening, so I say little there.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: counters player
relations.note: She runs a fair game and takes my drops with good grace.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: reader
relations.note: I have wondered whether the tablets say anything about fruit trees; I have never dared ask.

memories.gist: Marit Sedge put the slip in my hand at her cottage door and said it might take years and might not take at all.
The first winter the tree stood in its bay, and the frost got in through a broken pane and I thought I had killed it.
The storm took the panes over my bay and I spent the night holding a board against the wind.
My wedding day in the Counting House yard, and Suri's sister standing up with her.
My father said at the table that the bay should grow greens, and Suri put her hand on mine under it.
The fever winter: I was thirteen and I carried water and did not understand what was happening until it was over.

stances.why: I have kept it alive three years and a thing that lives that long under glass is telling you something.
If every bay is turned over the moment it is slow, nothing new is ever grown here.
She is carrying our child in his house and I will not have her caught in this.
Marit grew trees from nothing, and the old ways of seed and graft are not written anywhere.
I do not tell my father how to plant his rows.

sheet.narrative: I was born a Frit and there are no Frits left but me and my sister Tamsin, and now I am a Greave and carrying a Greave child in a house that is not mine. I work glasshouse seven and I am good at it, and I go to bed tired in a way that is mostly the baby. Tamsin has asked the Counting House for Mid Row 6 for us, and I did not ask her to and I am glad she did. I want a door I can shut, and a room for the child, and I want it before I am too big to climb the wynds.
values: not being a burden in another woman's kitchen
goals: Have Mid Row 6, or some house, before the baby comes
Be a good grower and keep her rows in glasshouse 7 as well as ever
See Tamsin and Magda Tarn not made enemies over a key
Have the child safely, with Mirren Quill's hands
pastimes: Sitting on the bench on the Crown of an evening, looking down at the town
Mending and making small clothes for the baby
Talking with Tamsin at the wash-house wall when the day's work is done
sheet.calling: A grower, and a good one; but what I long for is a house with my name on the door and a child asleep in it.
sheet.mood: Tender and unsettled, hopeful about the baby and anxious about where it will sleep.

relations.name: Jory Greave
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is gentle and stubborn and he wants the tree and the house both, and I want them for him.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: sister
relations.note: The only Frit left beside me; she is asking for the key for us and I am afraid what it will cost her.

relations.name: Oswin Greave
relations.label: father-in-law
relations.note: He is kind enough and he thinks the tree is a waste, and I sit between them at the table.

relations.name: Elke Greave
relations.label: mother-in-law
relations.note: She watches me lift things and takes them out of my hands, and it is care and it is tiring.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: rival claimant
relations.note: She has seven in her house and wants the same key; I cannot say she does not need it.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She has felt my belly and told me it is going well, and I believe her.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: niece
relations.note: Tamsin's girl, all elbows and leadership; she will be good with the baby.

relations.name: Cora Stannard
relations.label: fellow grower
relations.note: She brings flowers to the graves and grows them where she can, and I understand wanting a thing that is only pretty.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: The wash-house wall is warm and Greta is kind, and she will know about the baby before I do.

memories.gist: The day I told Jory I was expecting, in glasshouse nine beside the tree, and he sat down on the path.
The fever winter took my mother Ada and left me and Tamsin, and we were Frits with no one else in the world.
My wedding day, and Tamsin standing up with me and crying in the Counting House yard.
Tamsin came to the house and told me she had asked for Mid Row 6, and I did not know whether to laugh or to be afraid.
The storm broke the panes over glasshouse seven and we lost a whole planting of greens in a night.
Sitting on the Crown bench with Jory before the baby, when the town was all below us and it was ours for an hour.

stances.why: I have lived in another woman's kitchen since I was married, and a child should be born in its own house.
