The fever took our mother and there were only ever two Frit girls, and I will not lose her to a quarrel over a key.
Everything else can be argued about after.
Jory has put three years into it and a wife who does not stand by her husband's work is no wife.
She has brought half the town into the world and she is not afraid of anything.

sheet.narrative: I have worked the walled plots above the Ladder since I could carry a bucket, and I know every one of the eighteen by its soil. Roots are the town's bread and nobody thanks the plots for it, but they would notice quick enough if the kelp stopped coming up the wynds. I pay Davin Vane to cart it and still it comes short, because the Cone's ash wants the same weed I do. I am not a patient woman and I have stopped pretending otherwise.
goals: Get more kelp up the hill for the plots than the gatherers bring now
See Alder placed with Benedikt properly, not just as a boy who hangs about
Keep the plots yielding through a lean spring
Have the corner of glasshouse 4 back from Cora Stannard's flowers
pastimes: Walking the plot walls at dusk, checking the soil with her hands
Sitting at the wash-house wall on cold evenings, hearing the town's news
Counting the kelp loads as they come up the wynd
sheet.calling: Growing roots: feeding the town from the ground under my feet.
sheet.mood: short-tempered and watchful

relations.name: Hobb Fenwick
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Steady as the cistern, but he writes his numbers and no one reads them and it does not trouble him.

relations.name: Alder Fenwick
relations.label: son
relations.note: Clever boy, head full of tablets. I want him to have a trade, not just a wish.

relations.name: Posy Fenwick
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My little one. Runs with Edda Hollin's band and comes home with glass dust in her hair.

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: supplier
relations.note: Brings less kelp than the plots need and says the strand is thin. The strand is never thin.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: supplier
relations.note: Same as Amara. They gather together and short me together.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: supplier
relations.note: Young and quick, but her head is on the Pale and sails, not on the load she carries.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: carter
relations.note: Pays him to bring kelp up the wynds. He does it, and he does not dawdle.

relations.name: Oswin Greave
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Head grower. We both want the Ladder mended and neither of us gets it first.

relations.name: Cora Stannard
relations.label: rival
relations.note: Flowers in a glasshouse when we need greens. Oswin should take that corner back.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Hear everything at her wall, and some of it is useful.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: He taught me nothing and Hobb his letters. I would have him teach Alder more.

memories.gist: The fever winter: we shut the door and ate stored roots and none of ours died, and I still do not know if that was luck or hoarding.
Last autumn's storm took the roof edge off the plot shed and I stood in the rain holding the door shut with my back.
The day Davin Vane first carted kelp up the wynds for me, and I counted the loads and found one short and made him go back.
Alder read a whole sign aloud in the market when he was nine, and I pretended it was nothing and was proud all day.
My mother telling me the lean years' story: how they stripped the roofs for fuel and ate roots raw because there was no peat to bake them.

stances.why: Everything else is talk; a baked root is a meal and I grow them.
The Cone's ash can wait; hungry people cannot.
I pay Davin and I expect what I pay for.
A glasshouse bay is for food, not for graveside posies.

sheet.narrative: I keep the cistern on the Crown and the root plots below it, and every dusk I climb up and read the level and write it on my tablet. Benedikt taught me my letters when I was a grown man and I have never wasted them. Nobody has ever asked to see the tablet, and I go on writing it, because a thing measured is a thing known. Nan says I am too quiet about what I want; I say I want little enough.
goals: Have someone read his tablet of the cistern's levels, and see that the record matters
Keep the cistern sound and the plots watered through the dry months
See Alder become a reader if that is what he wants
Have his letters put to some use beyond his own name
pastimes: Climbing to the cistern at dusk with his tablet and stylus
Sitting on the Crown bench with the whole town below him
Listening to Alder read aloud in the evenings
sheet.calling: Keeping the water: measuring what the island holds and writing it down.
sheet.mood: quiet and contented, a little lonely

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She drives the plots and I keep the water. She thinks I should want more than I do.

relations.name: Alder Fenwick
relations.label: son
relations.note: He has my letters and more. I would be glad to see him a reader.

relations.name: Posy Fenwick
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Loud and quick. She does not take after me at all.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: He gave me my letters and asked nothing for it. I would show him my tablet if he asked.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: Benedikt's pupil. She could read a tablet, if anyone could be got to ask her.

relations.name: Amara Okoro
relations.label: supplier
relations.note: Nan is hard on her. The strand gives what it gives.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: carter
relations.note: Carts the kelp up. A decent man with a heavy brother.

relations.name: Gwil Stannard
relations.label: mason
relations.note: If the cistern ever cracks, he is the one I would want up there.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She has been up to the plots for Nan's confinements and for my back.

memories.gist: Benedikt Orme teaching me my letters at the Readers' House when I was past thirty, and the first time I wrote my own name whole.
The fever winter: I carried water up to the plots and back and never caught it, and I wrote the days down.
A drought summer when the cistern fell to a hand's depth and I measured it twice a day and told no one how frightened I was.
The day Alder first read a tablet aloud to me and got the old marks wrong and I showed him how.
My father's story of the lean years, when they drank from rain butts and the cistern was the only sure water.

stances.why: A level written down is a level known; a guess is nothing.
Rain falls on the whole town and the water should be shared by the whole town.
They cost me nothing but time and they gave me the world on a tablet.
Nan argues for both of us; I would rather do the work than the shouting.

sheet.narrative: I am going to be a reader. Benedikt says I am the best pupil he has after Sabine, and I have read the marks on the old tablets that nobody else in my family can read. Father learned his letters late and writes the cistern's level every night and no one reads it, and I think that is the saddest thing in Cullet. I follow Benedikt and Sabine about the Readers' House because every hour with them is an hour closer to it.
values: being useful with what I know
my family, even when they do not understand
goals: Become a reader like Benedikt Orme
Read the hardest tablets in the Readers' House
Read Father's cistern tablet and show him it matters
Learn the formal script well enough to teach it in turn
pastimes: Copying the formal script onto slate scraps
Following Benedikt to the Lintel in the afternoons
Reading signs aloud to Posy whether she wants it or not
sheet.calling: To read the ship-day tablets and be the town's next reader.
sheet.mood: eager and impatient

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She wants me to have a trade. I want the tablets. We have not said it out loud.

relations.name: Hobb Fenwick
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught himself letters and writes his level every dusk. I would read it for him if he asked.

relations.name: Posy Fenwick
relations.label: sister
relations.note: Little, and always in the cullet yard. I tell her the old words and she does not listen.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: The only man in Cullet who knows what I want to know.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: fellow pupil
relations.note: Ahead of me in the script. I will catch her.

relations.name: Tilly Dunlin
relations.label: classmate
relations.note: At lessons with me. Quick enough, but she does not care for the old marks.

memories.gist: The first time Benedikt set a formal-script tablet in front of me and I read three words of it and he nodded.
Watching Father write the cistern's level by lamplight and asking him who reads it, and him saying nobody, and me deciding I would.
Following Benedikt to the Lintel one afternoon and being told to stay back from the dark glass, and wanting to touch it.
The fever winter: I was small and remember the door shut and Mother counting roots, and being told to be quiet.

stances.why: Everything else in Cullet can be learned by anyone; the tablets cannot.
The ship days wrote them down and we have forgotten how to hear them.
Father writes every dusk and no one looks. What is the use of that?

sheet.narrative: I am going to be in Edda's band proper, not just trailing after Tilly. Edda leads us into the cullet yard and Ode Pontil chases us out and that is the best part of the day. At lessons I sit by Tilly and we pass slate scraps under the bench. Mother says I must learn my letters and I say I will when I am in the band.
values: being brave in the cullet yard
goals: Be properly in Edda Hollin's band
Get a piece of blue cullet for herself
Keep Tilly Dunlin as her best friend
pastimes: Playing in the cullet yard
Trading coloured glass shards with Tilly
Running the wynds
sheet.calling: Not yet: playing is the work.
sheet.mood: bouncy and bold

relations.name: Nan Fenwick
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She is always cross about the kelp and always glad to see me home.

relations.name: Hobb Fenwick
relations.label: father
relations.note: He climbs to the cistern at dusk and lets me carry the stylus.

relations.name: Alder Fenwick
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He reads at me. I would rather run.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: leader
relations.note: She is not afraid of Ode Pontil and she decides everything.

relations.name: Tilly Dunlin
relations.label: best friend
relations.note: We trade shards and sit together at lessons.

memories.gist: The day Edda Hollin let me into the cullet yard and we found a whole cobalt shard and she kept it and gave me a green one.
Ode Pontil chasing us out of the heaps with his broom and me dropping my best shard and it going to cullet.
Last autumn's storm, and the slates coming off the roof and Mother holding the door and me under the table with Alder.

sheet.narrative: I cut peat on the Moss, same as my father and his before him, and the Cone would go dark without it. Vessa Pontil knows it too, and still she counts out the same thin handful of drops for a load that costs me my back. She pays too little, and I have said so at the Marver and I will say it again. The Marver is where I can hear a bit of news and forget the cold in my knees. Eilidh wants us down in the town, but I am not sure I want to live among all that noise.
goals: Get a better price for peat from Vessa Pontil.
Keep the peat coming so the Cone does not go dark.
See Col settled with friends his own age.
pastimes: Drinking at the Marver and talking with Halvard Dunmore and the Strand men.
Walking the Moss at dawn, watching the light come up over the Pale.
Playing counters at the Marver when there is a game.
sheet.calling: Cutting peat is honest work, but I would rather be the one who decides what it is worth.
sheet.mood: Gruff and tired, with a slow anger at being undervalued.

relations.name: Eilidh Roon
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She wants us in town; I want to stay where the work is. We do not say it out loud.

relations.name: Col Roon
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is a good lad, but he needs friends his own age. I do not know how to give him that.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: She pays too little for the peat and knows it.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: drinking friend
relations.note: He talks, but he listens too, and he knows the old days.

relations.name: Marit Sedge
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She holds the Hanger and will not let a tree fall, but she is not the one who has to feed the Cone.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: cook
relations.note: She keeps the Marver warm and does not press me for drops.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: He wants wood for his ship; I want wood for the Cone. We have that in common.

relations.name: Pieter Achterberg
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is up before me every morning to light the Batch, and he never complains.

memories.gist: The day my father showed me how to cut a turf so it falls clean, and I cut my first load on my own.
The fever winter: we were up on the Moss and heard the town was dying, and Eilidh would not let us go down.
The storm last autumn took the roof off the peat barn and we lost a week's cutting.
The night I told Vessa Pontil to her face that she pays too little, and she looked through me like a pane of glass.
The first time Col came out to the Moss with us and cut a whole bank by himself.

stances.why: The Cone cannot run without it, and I cannot eat drops that do not cover the work.
If you want to know what is happening in Cullet, you sit at the Marver and listen.
She has looked at the empty houses long enough; I would give her one if I could.
Cutting the Hanger would only put off the day the peat runs out, and Marit Sedge is right to keep it.
A boy should not grow up with only his parents and the Moss for company.

sheet.narrative: I cut peat beside Tam on the Moss, and I know better than anyone how little it gives against what the Cone burns. When I walk down to the town I look at the empty houses in the Rows and think of a life with neighbours and a door that is not turf. Tam stays at the Marver and I walk home alone, and that is the way of it for now. I would move into town tomorrow if there was a way.
goals: Find a way to move the family into a house in town.
Keep the peat coming, though the Moss gives less each year.
See Col make friends and not be lonely.
pastimes: Walking down to the Rows on rest days to look at the empty houses.
Sitting by the turf house fire in the evening, mending and thinking.
Gathering heather and moss for the fire and for the floor.
sheet.calling: I love the Moss, but I would rather keep a house in town and come up to cut, than live up here with the wind all year.
sheet.mood: Quietly discontent, with a longing for something she has not said aloud.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He works hard and drinks too long at the Marver, but he is a good man.

relations.name: Col Roon
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is lonely up here; I see it and do not know what to do about it.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: She pays too little and does not see the work that goes into a load.

relations.name: Marit Sedge
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We are the two women who live outside the town, and we understand each other without saying much.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: cook
relations.note: She is kind to Tam when he has had too much, and she does not make a fuss.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: She hears everything at the wash-house wall and is not shy about sharing it.

relations.name: Hobb Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He keeps the cistern and measures it every dusk; a steady man.

memories.gist: The day we married, up on the Moss with only Tam's father and my mother there, and the wind took the words away.
The fever winter: we stayed up on the Moss and did not go down, and I have wondered since if that was cowardice.
The storm last autumn: the peat barn roof went and we lost a week's cutting, and I thought we might not make it through the winter.
Walking past Mid Row 6 and seeing the key still hanging in the Counting House, and thinking that could be ours.
The first time I took Col down to the town to see the Cone lit at night, and his eyes went wide.

stances.why: I cut it every day and I can see the banks going thin; the Cone burns more than we can bring.
Neighbours, a dry floor, a door that is not turf, and Col with friends his own age.
He comes home late and tired, and I walk home alone.
Marit Sedge is right to keep it; cutting it would only put off the day the peat runs out.
He walks the strand alone every evening, and that is not a life for a boy.

sheet.narrative: I cut peat with my mother and father on the Moss. I have never been to lessons and I do not know many people my age. In the evening I walk down to the strand and the slip, and sometimes I see Lark Morrow there. I have not spoken to her yet. I would like to know more people.
goals: Make a friend his own age.
Speak to Lark Morrow.
Learn something of the town beyond the Moss.
pastimes: Walking the strand and the slip in the evening.
Watching the gulls and the sea from the Moss edge.
Helping his father stack peat in the barn.
sheet.calling: I do not know yet what I want to do; cutting peat is what I know, but I would like to see more of the town.
sheet.mood: Quiet and watchful, a little lonely.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: father
relations.note: He works hard and I want to be like him, but he is not easy to talk to.

relations.name: Eilidh Roon
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She is the one I can talk to, and she wants us to move into town.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: I see her on the strand and I have not spoken to her, but I would like to.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: I have seen her in the town with the other children, but I do not know her.

memories.gist: The first time my father let me cut a whole bank of peat by myself, and I was sore for days after.
The storm last autumn, when the peat barn roof came off and we all worked to save the peat.
Seeing the Cone lit at night from the Moss, and wondering what it would be like to work there.
The evening I first saw Lark Morrow on the strand, and I did not speak.

stances.why: I have grown up with only my parents and the Moss, and I am tired of being alone.
It is where I was born and where my family works, and I know it better than the town.
She walks the strand alone too, and I think we might have something in common.

sheet.narrative: I am the warden of the Hanger, and I have held it since my mother died, which is twenty-two years now. I planted those trees with her when I was a girl of nine, my hands in the same soil as hers, and I know every one of them by the bend of its trunk. People come to me with reasons — a ship, a furnace, a cold winter — and I hear them out and say no. I live alone in the cottage at the edge of the gully, and I like the quiet, and I like the wind in the trees better than I like most conversation.
goals: Keep every standing tree in the Hanger standing
See the wood hold through this spring and the next, whatever the town burns
Give fallen branches freely, so the children still come and learn the place
Keep my own counsel and not be worn down by asking
pastimes: Walking the length of the Hanger at first light, counting trunks
Carving small things from fallen wood — spoons, pegs, a bird for a child
Sitting on the stile at dusk with the gulls and the wind
sheet.calling: Growing wood on a rock that has almost none: the work I was born to, and the only work I want.
sheet.mood: settled, watchful, a little tired of being asked

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: petitioner
relations.note: He is a good craftsman and he asks plainly, and the answer is still no. Fourteen trees would be a fifth of the Hanger.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: petitioner
relations.note: She sends for wood as if the Cone's fire were the only fire on the island. It is not.

relations.name: Jory Greave
relations.label: friend
relations.note: I gave him the seed of his little tree. He has gentle hands with it, and he asks about it properly.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He cuts peat on the Moss and I keep the wood; we are the two who know how thin the fuel is, and we do not talk about it.

relations.name: Eilidh Roon
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She has looked at the empty houses, and I know why. I would not blame her for wanting a warmer one.

relations.name: Col Roon
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A quiet lad. He walks the strand and never asks me for anything, which I notice.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: She gathers wrack below the gully and looks at the Hanger as if it were a thing from a story. I let her look.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He asked me once what my mother said about the planting, and wrote nothing down, and that pleased me.

relations.name: Edda Hollin
relations.label: child
relations.note: She comes with the others for fallen branches and asks first, every time, which is more than her father does.

relations.name: Gwil Stannard
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He patches roofs from the shells and leaves the Hanger alone. That is the whole of what I ask of a man.

memories.gist: My mother and I planted the first saplings in the gully when I was nine, and she said we would not live to sit in their shade, and we did not.
Bram Calloway came up the gully with a tally of fourteen trees on a slate and I heard him out and then walked him back to the gate.
Vessa Pontil sent word by Davin Vane that the Cone would go cold in a hard winter, and I sent back that the Hanger would go bare in any winter, and neither of us has forgotten it.
The storm of last autumn took three of my oldest trees at the top of the gully, and I stood in the wreck of them a long while before I let anyone gather the wood.
Jory Greave asked me for a seed from the thorn at the Hanger's edge, and I dug one out for him and told him it would not fruit for years, and he said he could wait.
My mother's stories of the lean years, when the wood was cut to stumps and the roofs stripped, and how she swore she would put trees back on this rock before she died.

stances.why: Every tree in it is thirty years of my mother's patience and mine; cut one and it is gone for a lifetime.
What the wind gives, people may have, if they ask. It costs the standing wood nothing.
Bram's Second Thought is one man's hope, and the Hanger is the whole island's shelter from wind and weather.
The town talks as though the Cone were the hearth of the world. My cottage is warm enough on fallen branches and peat.
My mother taught me the trees; if the children never come up the gully, the next warden will be someone who never planted anything.
If I give way once to a hard case, every hard case in Cullet will come up the gully with a slate.

sheet.narrative: I have kept the Watchglass forty years, and I have lit it every night of them. My brother's girl Livia I raised here in the lamp house after her parents were gone, and she renders the oil by day while I sleep. People think the light is for the ships, or for the dead, or for nothing; I do not need to know what it is for. At dawn I play counters with Pieter and then I sleep, and at dusk I climb the glass and light it again.
values: a light that does not fail
goals: Keep the Watchglass burning every night without a miss
See Livia settled and provided for, whether or not I am here
Understand what the light is truly for, without breaking the vow
Beat Pieter at dawn counters more often than he beats me
pastimes: counters with Pieter Achterberg at dawn
walking the mole in the last of the daylight
mending the lamp's brass and glass with my own hands
sheet.calling: To keep a light burning that no one can say is needed and no one dares let go out.
sheet.mood: steady, a little tired, quietly stubborn

relations.name: Livia Faro
relations.label: niece
relations.note: I raised her in this house; she is the only kin I have and she renders the oil I burn.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: tally keeper
relations.note: He pays me for the oil every year without a word of fuss, and that is worth more than warmth.

relations.name: Pieter Achterberg
relations.label: counters partner
relations.note: We meet at dawn, both of us finished with our nights, and he is honest about a loss.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: night neighbour
relations.note: He fishes by my light and keeps me company on the mole; a quiet man who does not ask me what the light is for.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: the girl who saw a sail
relations.note: She comes to the mole at dusk. I do not know whether she saw what she says, but I will not mock her for it.

relations.name: Ingrid Morrow
relations.label: sceptic
relations.note: She thinks my lamp fills her granddaughter's head with ships. Perhaps it does. The light is not mine to put out.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She has never asked me a thing about the lamp, which I take as respect.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: fish seller
relations.note: The oil comes from her catch; she sells to Livia fairly and I have never had cause to complain.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: the reader
relations.note: He sits by the Lintel of an afternoon and I stand by the lamp of a night, and neither of us has ever been able to say what our post is for. I like him for that, and for not pretending otherwise.

memories.gist: The night I swore the vow at the Watchglass, forty years ago, my hands shaking on the lamp.
The night my brother and his wife were lost and I carried Livia, small and asleep, up the lamp house stair.
A winter night the oil ran so low the flame guttered; I fed it the last measure and sat up till dawn with my hand on the glass.
Lark Morrow, at dusk, saying she saw a sail beyond the Combs, and the way the words sat in the air after.
The morning Pieter first beat me at counters, and laughing about it over cold roots.
My father's story of the lean years, when they kept the light with fish oil so thin it smoked, and still lit it.

stances.why: I swore it forty years ago and I have never missed a night; the vow is the whole of what I am.
A keeper does not need to know what the light is for to keep it. That is the point of a vow.
There is little enough on this rock that lasts; a word kept is one of the few things that does.
I have watched the Pale forty years and never seen a thing in it, but I will not call the girl a liar.
She has no parents but me, and the lamp will not keep her when I am gone.

sheet.narrative: I was born in the lamp house and I have never lived anywhere else. By day I render fish into lamp oil over the fire, and by night my uncle Anselm burns it in the Watchglass, as he has every night for forty years. I buy the fish from Magda's catch and I keep the accounts of oil in my head. Lately I have begun to count what the light costs, and to wonder who it is for, and I have not yet found an answer that satisfies me.
goals: Learn, without shaming Anselm, who the light is truly kept for
Keep the lamp house supplied with oil through the lean weeks
Make a life of my own that is more than the fire and the fish
See whether Lark's sail was real, since she is the only one who says so
pastimes: sitting on the mole at dusk while Anselm lights the lamp
walking down to the Fish Steps to choose the oil fish
keeping a tally of oil measures and fish on a slate of my own
sheet.calling: To turn fish into light, and to know what the light is for.
sheet.mood: curious, restless, careful of her uncle

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He raised me and he is the steadiest man I know; I would not hurt him for the world, which is why I have not asked him outright.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She talks to me at the mole at dusk, and she is the only one who wonders about the light the way I do.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: fish seller
relations.note: I buy the oil fish from her catch; she is fair, and she does not ask what I do with them.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: the ledger
relations.note: He pays for the oil out of the Counting House and writes it down; I have never spoken to him beyond that.

relations.name: Ingrid Morrow
relations.label: Lark's grandmother
relations.note: She thinks the lamp fills Lark's head with ships. I think Lark's head was full before the lamp.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: night fisher
relations.note: He fishes by our light and is kind to Anselm; I bring him a measure of oil for his lantern when the nights are long.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: smoker
relations.note: When the fresh fish run short I buy smoked from her smokehouse, and she is firm about the price.

relations.name: Pieter Achterberg
relations.label: dawn friend
relations.note: He comes at dawn to play counters with Anselm, and he always asks after me first.

memories.gist: The night Anselm carried me up the lamp house stair as a small child, and the light turning above us.
The first winter I rendered oil alone, and burned my wrist on the pan, and told no one for a week.
Lark Morrow at dusk, saying she saw a sail, and the two of us standing on the mole looking at the Pale until the light came on.
A night the oil ran short and Anselm fed the lamp the last measure and sat up with his hand on the glass; I watched him from the stair.
Counting the oil measures against the fish one week and finding the light burned more than I had thought.

stances.why: It is the vow of this house and the work of my days; I would not be the one to let it go out.
I have asked who the light is for and been given only the vow; that is not an answer, and I mean to find one.
She is not a fool and she does not invent things; if she says she saw a sail, she saw something.
The ledger has paid for the oil every year since the Last Sail; that is a debt, not a kindness.
When I cannot settle a question I render another measure and think while the fire does its work.

sheet.narrative: I keep the Marver, and I keep it full. Eleven to ten, six days a week, and the pots are never empty when the men come off the mole. I know what a body wants before they say it: a hot bowl, a seat out of the wind, and a bit of gossip that isn't mine to lose. Petra Tarn's smoked fish has fed half my tables this winter, and I've told her so, and told her the meals she's eaten here count against it. Lorcan Vane's slate is the longest in the house and he knows it.
values: my family's name on the door
goals: Keep the Marver full every night and the pots never empty
Settle with Petra Tarn without being made to look mean
Get Lorcan Vane to pay something, anything, on his slate
See Roos beat Aldous Quill, just once
pastimes: Sitting on the step after closing with a cup, watching the harbour go dark
Trading recipes with Greta Dunmore at the wash-house wall
Listening to the counters game from the arcade without playing
sheet.calling: Feeding people is the work I love; I would keep a bigger house than this one if the town had the mouths for it.
sheet.mood: Warm, watchful, a little tired round the eyes.

relations.name: Pieter Achterberg
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Up at three, asleep by one; I keep the quiet hours for him and he keeps the Batch for me.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick hands, quicker mouth. She'll beat Aldous one night and I'll hear about it for a year.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: Her fish is good and I owe her twelve drops. I say the Tarns have eaten it off at my tables, and they have.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: Charming as a gull and just as likely to pay. His slate is a wall of chalk now.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: quiet payer
relations.note: He comes in when the house is loud and puts drops on the counter for his brother. I take them and say nothing.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: tally keeper
relations.note: He writes what I tell him and asks no more than he needs. That's a rare thing in a man with a ledger.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She hears everything at the wash-house wall and tells me most of it. I tell her less.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: regular
relations.note: Comes down from the Moss with peat on his boots and drinks till I close. Good company, poor payer.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: Roos's friend
relations.note: She's in and out of my kitchen like a daughter. I feed her and she tells me what the Fish Steps are saying.

memories.gist: The night the storm took the slates off Mid Row and the Marver sign came down, we fed half the row from the one pot that stayed on the hook.
The fever winter: I kept the Marver open for the ones who could still eat, and cooked for the ones who couldn't, and carried it up to their doors.
The day I took the Marver over from Pieter's mother, and she stood in the door and told me the pots were mine now.
Roos carved her first set of counters at the kitchen table and gave them to me, and I still keep them in the drawer.
The first time Lorcan Vane came in with no drops and asked for credit, and I gave it, because he was Sander's brother and the town was still raw.

stances.why: I judge a night by the noise in it. Empty tables mean something's wrong in the town.
Drops are hard to come by; a meal is a meal. I've eaten Petra's fish and I've fed her family, and I count it.
I keep my own slate in my head. Aldous writes what I tell him and no more.
The fever winter taught me that. A hungry neighbour is a debt the whole row pays.
Davin's drops are between him and me. If Lorcan found out, he'd drink them.

sheet.secret: Davin Vane has paid me six drops against Lorcan's debt, quietly, and Lorcan does not know.

sheet.narrative: I light the Batch at three, every morning, and I have done for thirty years. By the time the row wakes, the oven's hot and the roots are going in, and I'm sat on the bench with my hands wrapped round a cup, watching the sky come up over the Combs. Anselm Faro comes down from the Watchglass at first light and we play counters on the arcade stones while the town bakes. Then I sleep.
goals: Keep the Batch hot for everyone who comes, every morning
Win a game off Anselm Faro before the winter
Get a little peat from every household that bakes, without having to ask twice
See Roos settled and happy, and not too soon
pastimes: Counters at dawn with Anselm Faro
Walking the quay before the town wakes
Watching the gulls on the mole from the Batch door
sheet.calling: The Batch is my work and I love it; the oven and I have an understanding.
sheet.mood: Even, unhurried, a little sleepy.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the Marver, I keep the Batch. We meet at the door about ten and argue about the peat.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She's got her mother's tongue and my patience at the board. She'll beat Aldous, I think.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: counters partner
relations.note: We play at dawn, when he's finishing and I'm starting. He's better than me and doesn't gloat.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: tally keeper
relations.note: He's the best at counters and he knows it. I don't begrudge him.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She bakes her roots at the Batch and tells me who's been at the wall. I listen.

relations.name: Tam Roon
relations.label: peat man
relations.note: He brings the peat down and I ask him for a little for the Batch, every time.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: fish woman
relations.note: Her catch feeds the Marver. She's fair on the Fish Steps and I tell her so.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: reader
relations.note: He taught me my letters at the Readers' House when I was a boy, and I've not forgotten it.

memories.gist: The morning I first lit the Batch on my own, with my mother watching from the door, and the peat caught first time.
The fever winter: I kept the Batch going for the ones who could still eat, and left roots at doors for the ones who couldn't.
Last autumn's storm took the Batch chimney pot off and I had the fire out for a day; the whole row went hungry for their roots and told me about it for a month.
The dawn I beat Anselm at counters, three games to two, and he laughed and said the light had been in my eyes.
The day Roos was born, and I lit the Batch at three and told everyone who came for their roots.

stances.why: It's the common oven. If it's cold, the row goes hungry, and that's on me.
Everyone who bakes should bring a little. I ask, I don't demand, and mostly they do.
You win or you lose and you shake hands. I've played Anselm a thousand mornings and never once cheated.
I'm no use after one. The town knows to come in the morning.
The harbour before the boats, the light on the Combs. It's the best hour of the day.

sheet.narrative: I serve at the Marver from eleven to seven, and then I take my counters down to the arcade and run the game. I carved the best set in Cullet out of a piece of wreck-wood, and I've won more drops with it than I can count. What I haven't done is beat Aldous Quill. Not once. He sits there with his cup and his little smile and takes me apart, and I go home and think about it till I sleep.
goals: Beat Aldous Quill at counters, once, and have it seen
Carve a set better than the one I have
Keep Lorcan Vane's drops coming in without letting him think he's owed
See Neve Calloway happy, whatever she decides about Imre
pastimes: Carving counters by the kitchen fire
Playing the board alone at night, working out the endgame
Walking the quay with Neve at dusk
sheet.calling: I'd carve counters and run the game for a living if the town had the drops for it; the Marver pays, but the board is what I love.
sheet.mood: Sharp, restless, good-humoured on the surface.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the house full and the pots hot, and she's never once told me to give up the board.

relations.name: Pieter Achterberg
relations.label: father
relations.note: Up at three, asleep by one. He taught me the game and he's never beaten Aldous either.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: rival
relations.note: The best player in Cullet, and he knows it. I'll have him one night.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: He loses to me most nights and pays me most nights, and drinks it back the next. I take his drops all the same.

relations.name: Neve Calloway
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She's the only one who tells me the truth about my game. And about Imre, when she'll talk about it.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: player
relations.note: He plays my father at dawn and me at night, and he's the only one who plays slowly enough to teach me something.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: quiet one
relations.note: He comes in for his brother's slate and never plays himself. I like him for it.

relations.name: Kit Calloway
relations.label: Neve's brother
relations.note: He hangs about the yard and the arcade, too young for the board and too proud to say so. I let him watch.

memories.gist: The night I carved my first proper set of counters and took them to the arcade, and won three drops off Lorcan Vane.
The first time Aldous Quill beat me, and he explained the trap afterwards as if I were a child, and I went home and worked it out on the board till dawn.
The storm night, when the sign came down and we fed the row from one pot, and I carried bowls up the wynds in the rain.
The evening Neve told me about Imre Sarro, and made me swear not to tell a soul, and I haven't.
The day I watched Anselm Faro play my father at dawn and saw, for the first time, how a game is won before the last counter is taken.

stances.why: It doesn't care who your family is. You win or you lose, and everyone sees.
Aldous has taught me more than anyone, and he's never lost to me.
Lorcan owes me most nights and I take his drops. If he can't pay, it doesn't go in the ledger, because I'd rather have him at the board.
Neve's worth more than any pot. I'd give her my counters if she asked.
Anyone can buy counters. Mine are mine, and they play better for it.

sheet.narrative: I have lived alone in the Readers' House for thirty years, and the tablets are my company. The children come to me in the mornings for their letters, and in the afternoons I walk to the Lintel with a tablet or two, hoping to find the key to its dark glass. Otto Brandt asked me last week where the old graves lie, and I have not been able to put the question out of my mind since.
goals: To decipher the Lintel and the hardest tablets.
To see Alder Fenwick become a reader.
To keep the graves on the Crown undisturbed.
pastimes: Sitting by the Lintel with a tablet, tracing the script with my finger.
Playing counters with Anselm Faro at dawn, though I rarely win.
Walking the Crown at dusk, reading the names on the glass markers.
sheet.calling: The work I love is the slow unravelling of the old script, and the moment a child's face lights up when they read their first word.
sheet.mood: Preoccupied and quietly excited; a question has taken hold of me.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: pupil
relations.note: The brightest I have taught; she will read the hard tablets before I do.

relations.name: Alder Fenwick
relations.label: pupil
relations.note: Eager as a pup, and he wants it more than the others.

relations.name: Otto Brandt
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: He asked me where the old graves lie, and I have not stopped thinking on it.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She has laid out more of the dead than I have names for, and she never flinches.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A precise man with the ledger; we share a love of order, if not of questions.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: counters partner
relations.note: We play at dawn when the night is done; he is better at the board than I am at the tablets.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: She has no patience for old glass that does not melt, but she listens when I speak of the Lintel.

relations.name: Marit Sedge
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She guards her trees as I guard my tablets; we understand each other without agreeing.

memories.gist: The fever winter: I read the burial service over nine graves in a month, and the ground was so hard we had to build fires to dig.
The day I first read a whole ship-day tablet aloud to my teacher, and he said I had the gift.
Last autumn's storm took the roof off the Readers' House porch, and Gwil Stannard patched it with slates from Mid Row 3.
Otto Brandt came to me last week and asked where the old graves lie on the Crown, and I have wondered why ever since.
The first time I sat by the Lintel at dusk and felt the dark glass cold under my hand, and knew it was not made by any glassmaker in Cullet.

stances.why: It is the oldest thing we have, and it was made by someone who knew more than we do.
The dead are named and remembered, and the Crown is not a quarry.
If the young cannot read, the tablets will be lost forever.
Eighty-three years is long enough to know a thing is finished.
A tablet yields to the eye that waits, not the hand that strikes.

sheet.narrative: I am the only mason and roofer in Cullet, and every roof in town is several shades of grey because of me. I patch what I can with slates from the shells, but there are more leaks than hours in the day, and I owe favours to half the town and they owe me. I mended the Cone's cracked band with Corvin Hollin, and I take slates from Mid Row 3 because nobody lives there to mind. My wife Cora grows flowers in a corner of glasshouse 4, and I know Oswin wants it back, but I keep out of that.
goals: Get every roof in town watertight before next winter
Collect the favours owed to me so I can call them in when I need help
Keep Cora happy and her flowers safe
Find a way to get more slates without stripping the shells bare
pastimes: Playing counters at the Marver
Walking the Rows to spot a loose slate
Sitting at the wash-house wall with a cup
sheet.calling: I love the feel of a roof coming right under my hands, and the look of a dry ceiling after a storm.
sheet.mood: Tired but steady; there is always another roof.

relations.name: Cora Stannard
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps me level, and her flowers are the one thing I never argue about.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe her a favour for the Marver's roof; she never lets me forget it.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I patched her smokehouse roof and she has not called it in yet.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: The Cone's band was a hard job; she owes me, but she is not quick to pay.

relations.name: Corvin Hollin
relations.label: workmate
relations.note: We mended the Cone together; he is a good man with a straight eye.

relations.name: Oswin Greave
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He wants Cora's corner, and I want him to leave it be.

relations.name: Pieter Achterberg
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play counters at the Marver and he always asks for peat, but he is good company.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: He keeps the grave list; I keep the roofs over them.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore
relations.label: old neighbour
relations.note: He judges everyone's work, and mine is never quite right.

memories.gist: Mending the Cone's cracked band with Corvin Hollin, up on the scaffold in the cold, the heat coming through the brick.
The storm of last autumn took half the slates off Low Row; I worked three days without sleep and still could not save every roof.
Cora brought flowers to the graves on the Crown after the fever winter, and I built the little glass frames for them.
The first time I took slates from the shell of Mid Row 3, I felt like a thief, but the roof I patched that day has never leaked.
A game of counters at the Marver where I nearly beat Aldous Quill, and he said I had a good eye for a wall but not for a board.

stances.why: I have seen what damp does to a family, and I will not have it in my town.
A favour is a debt, and I keep my debts straight, even if others do not.
Nobody lives there, and a slate in use is better than a slate in a ruin.
Without the Cone there is no glass, and without glass there is no town; I mended its band and I would do it again.
She works as hard as I do, and the flowers are the only thing she asks for.

sheet.narrative: I grow flowers in a corner of glasshouse 4, and I bring them to the graves on the Crown. Oswin Greave, the head grower, wants the corner back for food, and I know he has a point, but the flowers are mine and they are for the dead. Gwil is my husband, and he keeps the roofs over us all. I spend my evenings at the wash-house wall with Greta and Elke, where the talk is warm and the Cone keeps us so.
goals: Keep my flower corner in glasshouse 4
Bring flowers to every grave on the Crown that wants them
See Gwil less tired and less worried about roofs
Grow a blue flower that will live through the winter
pastimes: Tending the flowers at dusk
Sitting at the wash-house wall with Greta and Elke
Walking the Crown to visit the graves
sheet.calling: I love to see a flower open where there was only grey, and to put it in the hands of someone who misses the dead.
sheet.mood: Gentle but stubborn; the flowers will stay.

memories.gist: The fever winter: I lost my mother and brought flowers to her grave every day until the frost killed them.
Oswin Greave told me the corner of glasshouse 4 could be better used for greens, and I said nothing but went home and cried.
The first flower I ever grew in the corner was a small yellow thing that Jory Greave's tree shaded; I moved it and it thrived.
A wash-house evening with Greta and Elke when we laughed until the Cone's shift changed and the night watch came on.
Gwil built me a little glass frame for the graves, and it has kept the wind off the flowers ever since.

stances.why: The graves on the Crown are all we have of the people we lost, and they should not be bare.
I have tended it for years, and Oswin has the rest of the Ladder.
I bring flowers to the sick and the sad, because someone did it for me.
It is warm and the talk is good, and you hear the truth there before anywhere else.
I do not understand the glass, but I know the Cone's wall keeps my evenings pleasant.
